Setting (JSON key / CLI setting name) Type Default Description filter boolean false Enable/disable filtering (other settings only take effect when this is on) allow_type list all Comma-separated list of message types to allow (1-27) block_type list none Comma-separated list of message types to block allow_repeat list all Allow messages with specific repeat counter values (0-3); alias select_repeat block_repeat list none Block messages with specific repeat counter values allow_mmsi list all Only allow messages from specific MMSI numbers; alias select_mmsi block_mmsi list none Block messages from specific MMSI numbers allow_channel string all Only allow messages from specific AIS channels (e.g. AB); alias select_channel id list all Comma-separated list of station IDs to allow (0-999999); alias select_id gps boolean true Include GPS messages in output. Takes effect only with the filter on: FILTER on GPS off ais boolean true Include AIS messages in output remove_empty boolean false Drop messages whose JSON payload is empty after decoding

Downsampling options:

Setting (JSON key / CLI setting name) Type Default Description unique boolean false Only send/show unique messages position_interval number false Minimal time in seconds between position updates for a ship, off = false or 0 own_interval number false Minimal time in seconds between updates for own ship, off = false or 0

docs.title: Output Configuration
docs.text:
AIS-catcher has multiple output options. As for the input, they share a few common settings to manage the flow of messages to output connections and for filtering.

Key casing

JSON configuration keys are case-sensitive and should be lowercase. Command-line setting names are not case-sensitive; this documentation shows them in lowercase to match JSON.

docs.title: Message Filtering
docs.text: For detailed information about filtering options, see the Message Filtering page. Filtering allows you to control which messages are included in the output based on type, channel, MMSI, and other criteria.

docs.title: Routing Messages
docs.text: In principle, messages from all models sourced via all input connections flow to all output connections. Sometimes it is desirable to manage this flow: set groups_in on an output, listing the groups that should feed it.

docs.title: Output Options
docs.text: AIS-catcher offers multiple output options to suit different use cases. Below is an overview of the available output methods:

docs.title: Screen Output
docs.text: • Console Output: Display AIS messages directly in your terminal with customizable formats

docs.title: Network Output Options
docs.text:
• TCP Server: Run an AIS server that clients can connect to
  • TCP Client: Connect to remote AIS servers
  • UDP: Send AIS messages via UDP to specified destinations
  • HTTP: Provide AIS data through HTTP endpoints

docs.title: Integration Options
docs.text:
• Community Feed: Share your AIS data with the community
  • PostgreSQL: Write AIS messages to Postgres database
  • Web Viewer: Built-in web interface for visualizing vessel traffic
  • MQTT: Publish AIS data to MQTT brokers
  • NMEA2000: Interface with NMEA2000 networks

docs.title: Places
docs.text:
A place is a named piece of the map: a port, a berth, an anchorage, a stretch of water, or a zone you want to keep an eye on. Give AIS-catcher a directory of place files and the web viewer will show them on the map, tell you which ships are in each one, keep a record of every ship's visits, and announce arrivals and departures.

Places are optional. Without a place directory the viewer works as before.

docs.title: Switching places on
docs.text:
AIS-catcher -N 8100 PLACES /path/to/places

On the command line, PLACES is a setting of the web viewer (-N). In a JSON configuration it is the key places under tracking, see Tracking and services.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• On the map. Every place has a marker, and its outline appears when you point at it. Large ports show from far out, berths only close in (see Place types).
  • On a ship's card. The card says where the ship is now ("Gate Terminal") and lists its recent visits with entry time, exit time and duration.
  • On a place. Clicking a marker opens the ships of that place, in tabs: Inside, Left, Arrived, Visits, Nearby, and for a port Expected, the ships that report it as their destination.
  • In the ticker. A ship entering or leaving a port, a guard zone, a sector or a water is announced.

docs.title: A place file
docs.text:
A place is a GeoJSON Feature in a file ending in .geojson. This is a complete one:

{
  "type": "Feature",
  "id": "0f2e6b1a-3c4d-4e5f-8a9b-0c1d2e3f4a5b",
  "properties": {
    "schema_version": 3,
    "revision": 1,
    "name": "Kade 1",
    "place_type": "berth"
  },
  "geometry": {
    "type": "Polygon",
    "coordinates": [[[4.05, 52.05], [4.06, 52.05], [4.06, 52.06], [4.05, 52.05]]]
  }
}

One place per file is the usual layout, with the file named after the place's id. A file may also be a FeatureCollection holding many places. Coordinates are longitude, then latitude, in WGS84.

And a port with everything a port usually carries:

{
  "type": "Feature",
  "id": "b47898d6-5dfc-4334-88a0-ad1ff96355ff",
  "properties": {
    "schema_version": 3,
    "revision": 1,
    "name": "Rotterdam",
    "place_type": "port",
    "codes": { "unlocode": ["NLRTM"] },
    "aliases": ["Rotterdam Europoort"],
    "rank": 3
  },
  "geometry": { "type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[3.95, 51.88], [4.55, 51.88], [4.55, 52.0], [3.95, 52.0], [3.95, 51.88]]] }
}

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
The same rules are published as a JSON Schema in the source tree, frontend/packages/core/place.schema.json, for tools that write place files.

Property Required Description id yes A UUID in lowercase. It is the place's identity: the name, the type and the outline may all change, the id never does. Generate one with uuidgen (and lowercase it) or python3 -c "import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4())". It sits beside properties, not inside it. schema_version yes Always 3. revision yes 1 in a file you write yourself. The editor raises it on every save. name yes Up to 120 characters. place_type yes One of the place types. part_of no The id of the place this one lies in: a berth in its terminal, a terminal in its port. codes no Codes by scheme, each a list. unlocode is the one AIS-catcher uses: only a port may have it, and no two places may claim the same code. Other schemes are kept as written. aliases no Other names of a port, up to 64, matched against the destinations ships report. category no A free label of up to 60 characters, such as sea, strait or restricted. Shown in place of the type name for guard zones, sectors and waters. rank no 0 to 3: how prominent the place is on the map. See Place types. country no Two capital letters. Without it a port takes the first two letters of its UN/LOCODE, and any other place the country of what it is part of. redirect_to no The id of the place that replaced this one. See Changing the catalogue. no no A number the editor gives a place on its first save and never changes. Leave it out of files you write yourself.

Anything else you put in properties (an attributes object with notes, a source, references) is kept exactly as written and ignored by AIS-catcher, so a place file can also carry your own documentation.

docs.title: Place types
docs.text:
The type decides three things: whether a stay needs the ship to stop before it counts, whether a crossing is announced in the ticker and at which level, and from which zoom the marker shows.

Type For A visit needs a stop Announced Marker from zoom berth One place alongside yes no 14 mooring Buoys, dolphins, a mooring field yes no 12 terminal A terminal, a yard, a quay with one operator yes no 12 marina A yacht harbour yes no rank-based anchorage Where ships wait at anchor yes no rank-based section A basin or district of a port yes no 13 port The port as a whole yes routine rank-based guardzone Any zone you draw to be told who enters and leaves no notice rank-based sector A traffic or VTS sector no routine rank-based water A sea, strait, lake, river or canal no routine no marker

The ticker has three levels. A routine event is shown in its turn. A notice is marked with ⚠ and holds the strip longer: that is what a ship entering or leaving a guard zone gets, since a guard zone is what you asked to be told about. Urgent is kept for distress messages and never used for places.

Rank-based means the place's own rank decides: 3 shows the marker from zoom 7, 2 from zoom 9, 1 from zoom 11 and 0 (the default) from zoom 12. Give an anchorage the rank of its port if the two should appear together. The types with a fixed zoom ignore rank. A place with a drawn outline shows its marker from zoom 10 at the latest, whatever its rank. A water has no marker: its outline is drawn when you select it, for example from a ship's card.

Where a ship is inside several places at once, the card names them in the order of the table: the berth before the terminal, the terminal before the port, the port before the water, and the smaller place first among two of the same type.

docs.title: Outlines
docs.text:
geometry is a Polygon, a MultiPolygon, or a Point.

  • A polygon is what makes a place work: ships are inside it or not. Each ring is closed (the last position repeats the first), has at least three corners, and does not cross or touch itself. A hole lies inside its polygon.
  • A multipolygon is one place in several parts, such as a port on both banks of a river.
  • A point gives a marker and nothing more. No ship is ever inside a point, so it has no visits; its dialog shows the ships nearby and, for a port, the ships bound for it.
  • An outline that crosses the 180° meridian is split there into two parts.

A place holds up to 2,000 corners. A water may be larger: 2,000 per part and 16,000 in all. One place is limited to 512 KiB, the whole catalogue to four million corners.

docs.title: How visits are counted
docs.text:
• A position has to be believable. Only a validated position is used: one the ship can have reached from its previous one at no more than 60 knots, and, for a ship that reported itself stopped, one no more than 200 m from where it lay minutes before. A position that does not fit is left out; if the next one agrees with it, the ship really has moved and carries on from there. A single corrupted message with a wrong MMSI, a jump across the map, or an old position delivered late therefore never puts a ship in your port or takes it out of its berth.
  • A crossing is confirmed by the next position. A ship enters when two positions in a row, at least ten seconds apart, are inside; the entry time is that of the first. Leaving works the same way, and one stray position across the line changes nothing.
  • Silence does not end a stay. A ship that reports again after an hour or more is taken as found: if it is still inside, the stay goes on with its original entry time; if it has gone, the stay ended at the last position inside. No crossing time is made up for what nobody saw: in a place's list of ships such a time is shown as a bound, with < or >.
  • A call needs a stop. At a port and everything in it, a stay counts as a call once the ship has been seen stopped for a minute: slower than 0.5 knots, or slower than 1 knot while reporting itself moored or at anchor. A ship steaming through a port without stopping leaves no call behind. In a guard zone, a sector or a water every passage counts.
  • Ten visits per ship are kept: the places it is in now and its most recent calls. When the viewer keeps a backup file, they are saved in it and survive a restart.

docs.title: Destinations
docs.text: A ship's reported destination is matched to your ports: first by UN/LOCODE, then by a name or alias that fits exactly one port. Matching ignores case, spaces and punctuation, and never guesses from part of a name. The Expected tab of a port lists the ships that match and are not yet inside.

docs.title: Changing the catalogue
docs.text:
Place files are read when AIS-catcher starts. There is no file watcher, so restart after changing them. Until then, a place whose file changed is matched as it was loaded but its outline is not served, and the log says so once. A file that breaks a rule is skipped whole and the log says why:

Places: skipped 0f2e6b1a-3c4d-4e5f-8a9b-0c1d2e3f4a5b.geojson: Polygon edges cross or touch themselves
Places: loaded 412 definitions from /etc/AIS-catcher/places

Files written by earlier releases, with schema_version 1 or 2, load as they are. An area or a custom place is read as a guard zone, size as rank and area_subtype as category, and a port named by its UN/LOCODE becomes the place's parent once every file is loaded. The files themselves are left as they are. To convert a whole directory to schema 3, run scripts/migrate-places.py from the source tree.

Two things to know before removing a place:

  • Deleting a place also deletes the visits ships made to it.
  • Replacing it keeps them. Leave the old file where it is and add "redirect_to": "<id of the new place>" to its properties. The old place disappears from the map, and its visits, including stays under way, continue at the new one. Use this when two outlines of the same place are merged into one.

docs.title: Summary Settings
docs.text: Setting (JSON key / CLI setting name) Type Default Description places string - Directory of place files for the web viewer (CLI: -N <port> PLACES <directory>) place_geometry boolean on Serve each place's outline to the map. Off keeps the outlines private to this installation: markers, lists and visits still work. A term of a server's view: "view": { "place_geometry": false } (CLI: -N <port> PLACE_GEOMETRY off)

docs.title: Web Viewer
docs.text:
AIS-catcher -N port [setting value] ...

AIS-catcher includes a simple web interface. A live demo is available for East Boston, US. The web interface gratefully uses the following libraries: chart.js, chart.js annotation plugin, leaflet, Material Design Icons, tabulator, marked and flag-icons.

Make sure you use the latest version and start the web viewer as follows: 

AIS-catcher -N 8100
where 8100 is the port number. If your machine network name is raspberrypi, e.g., then enter raspberrypi:8100 in your browser. On the web page, you will find several sections with information related to the station and received messages.

For users wishing to include a station name and a link to an external website in the Statistics section: 

AIS-catcher -N 8100 station Southwood station_link http://example.com
This could be a useful option if you want to offer the interface externally. To display the reception range and distances from your station, provide the program with the station coordinates and permission to share the location with the web viewer: 
AIS-catcher -N 8100 lat 50 lon 3.141592 share_loc on
The last option share_loc (default is off) will allow the web viewer to access and display the location.

The user can make a page in markdown format. The content will be shown in the About tab of the web viewer: 

AIS-catcher -N 8100 about about.md
All these options can be captured in the configuration file (in a section with name server), see below.

docs.title: Menu structure
docs.text: The main menu behind the hamburger icon in the top left corner navigates between different functional areas. Context-sensitive menus, accessible through right-click, long press on iOS, or the vertical dot icon on the map, offer more functionalities. Here you can set options like activating the "dark mode" theme, displaying the station range on the map, locking/unlocking the map center, toggling text-only ship labels, decluttering ship labels, and viewing details of the last message received from a vessel, amongst others.

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
When AIS-catcher receives data containing a vessel's dimensions but can not determine the direction it is pointing (heading), it will display a circle that accommodates the ship's dimensions regardless of heading. Missing heading information is common for Class B ships. If there's a decent approximation available for the heading, such as course-over-ground above certain speeds, it will be used. Shapes plotted using this approximation will have a dashed border, indicating incomplete information. An example is the USS Constitution docked in Boston.

In the map section, clicking on a vessel will open a ship card with details of the vessel. For smaller screens it can be minimized in the top bar (via the ^ symbol or by clicking on the header bar). The ship card will open minimized on mobile devices. In its maximized form, users can choose which rows will be visible in the minimized state. Additional options, such as looking up the vessel on aggregator sites, are available by clicking the three-dot icon on the ship card header.

docs.title: Ship card fields
docs.text:
Most fields on the ship card are self-explanatory and come directly from the vessel's AIS messages. The less obvious ones:

Field Meaning In Range Number of other AIS stations the vessel's own transponder reports it is currently receiving (from the SOTDMA communication state, ITU-R M.1371). It describes the radio situation around the ship, not how well your station receives it. Only present in some transmissions, so it can be empty or update irregularly. RSSI Signal strength (in dB) of the vessel's last message as measured by your receiver. Drift Estimated frequency offset (ppm) of the last message, useful for calibrating an RTL-SDR dongle. Distance / Bearing Position of the vessel relative to your station location. Receiver / Sources The receiver (group) that delivered the most recent message, and all receivers that have contributed messages for this vessel — relevant when running multiple receivers or network inputs. Count / last signal Number of messages received from this vessel and the time since the most recent one. Sender Type of transmitter (Class A/B vessel, base station, aid-to-navigation, SAR aircraft, etc.), derived from the MMSI and message types. Destination / ETA Voyage data as entered by the crew; the ETA is specified in UTC by the AIS standard. Blue Sign Blue sign status for inland (river) vessels.

Clicking a row on the maximized ship card selects it as the row that remains visible when the card is minimized/collapsed, so you can pick the information that matters most to you for the compact view.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The web-interface shows a "validation" indication at the left border of the ship card header.

AIS-catcher analyzes an enormous stream of bits per day for both AIS channels (2 to the power 33 to be precise). To avoid erroneous messages, the AIS system employs a 16-bit CRC and matching of other bit patterns. Unfortunately, purely statistically this cannot prevent that there will be an occasional technically correct but nonsense message. These are typically easy to recognize (e.g. looking at the signal level, and location on the map) and aggregator sites like MarineTraffic will filter these out.

To reliably measure the reception range for the station in the web interface, AIS-catcher has implemented a "validation function" that checks the location of the vessel for consistency between messages and flags if there is an inconsistency. Practically speaking, if we receive a position from an MMSI that is relatively close to the last received position, the "validation" indicator will be green and the distance to the station will be included to determine the station range. Please note that messages within 50 NMi from the receiving station will always be included for range setting. The validation indicator will be grey if validation for the location cannot be performed and red if it is not successful.

docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
The Plot section contains several visualizations to assess the performance of the receiver:

Restarting AIS-catcher typically erases history in the graphs. To retain plot "state" and backup the information to a file use the following:

AIS-catcher -N 8100 file stat.bin backup 10
This will back up the plots when the program closes and every 10 minutes in a file stat.bin. The minimum backup interval is 5 minutes.

docs.title: Custom plugins and styles...
docs.text:
To give the user the option to tweak the look-and-feel and functionality of the web viewer and/or modify for example the color scheme or regional preferences, the program provides the option to inject custom plugins (JavaScript) and CSS into the website, with a command like: 

AIS-catcher -N 8100 plugin plugin1.js plugin plugin2.js style mystyle.css
You can also include all plugin files from a specific directory using the command: 
AIS-catcher -N 8100 plugin_dir /usr/share/aiscatcher/plugins
Files need to have the extension .pjs and .pss for respectively JavaScript and CSS style plugins. The repository includes a few example plugins that demonstrate how to add additional maps or cater to regional preferences. Examples of plugins can be found in another GitHub repository.

A plugin runs in the browser of everyone who opens the map: install only plugins you trust.

docs.title: Offline web viewer
docs.text:
The web viewer runs without an internet connection out of the box: all web libraries are now bundled into AIS-catcher, so no online content is fetched to render the interface. This facilitates using the web interface whilst traveling.

Offline maps can be included in mbtiles format: 

AIS-catcher  -N 8100 mbtiles filename
or as an overlay 
AIS-catcher  -N 8100 mboverlay filename

docs.title: Sending data to Prometheus for use in Grafana dashboards
docs.text:
You can add the option PROME on to the web configuration command to start rendering Prometheus-compatible statistics at /metrics. For example:

AIS-catcher -N 8100 prome on

Next to the station's figures (ais_stat_*, ais_msg_*), /metrics has a row per input and per output, labelled with input or output (its number), type and description (the description set on it, or a name such as UDP #1):

Metric Type Meaning ais_input_count counter Messages decoded from the input ais_input_bytes_in counter Raw bytes received ais_input_up gauge 1 while the input streams, else 0 ais_input_last_message_timestamp_seconds gauge Unix time of the last message decoded, 0 before the first ais_input_errors counter Messages with errors, by error: checksum, undersized, oversized ais_input_connect_ok, ais_input_connect_fail, ais_input_reconnects counter Connections made, failed and made again, for an input that dials a server (-t rtl_tcp or a TCP feed, -y SpyServer) ais_input_connected gauge 1 while such an input is connected ais_output_count counter Messages passed to the output after its filter ais_output_bytes_out, ais_output_bytes_in counter Bytes sent and received ais_output_dropped counter Messages the output could not send: no connection, a full queue or a failed send ais_output_connect_ok, ais_output_connect_fail, ais_output_reconnects counter Connections made, failed and made again, for an output that holds connections ais_output_connected gauge Connections the output holds now

The connection rows appear only for inputs and outputs that hold a connection.

For more information on how to configure Prometheus and Grafana to get an initial dashboard, see README-grafana.md.

docs.title: The API on the same port
docs.text:
The viewer is a server on the station's ships, the same server that offers the API, MCP, the system service, GeoJSON and Prometheus: each is a switch on -N. For example, the map, the API and MCP on port 8100:

AIS-catcher -N 8100 api on mcp on

A second -N is a second server on the same ships; ui off leaves the map out of one. A -N listens on every interface, as the viewer always did, so other machines on the network reach its map. One that serves the API, MCP or the system service stays on this machine instead, and says so in the log, unless it has keys, public on, or an ip_bind of its own; see Keys. An entry of services in a configuration file listens on this machine unless its bind says otherwise.

docs.title: The ship list for scripts (API v0)
docs.text: Next to the map, a server answers the ship list and the statistics as v0.70 did: /ships.json, /api/ships.json, /api/ships_full.json and /stat.json. The map does not read them; they are there for the scripts written against them. They are on for a -N and a server section, as before, and off for an entry of services unless it says "api_v0": true. api_v0 off takes them away from a -N. limited does not cap them: they answer every ship in full, so on a limited server switch api_v0 off unless those lists are meant to be read. New scripts are better served by the API.

docs.title: Several stations in one viewer
docs.text:
The receivers of one AIS-catcher stand at stations (stations in a configuration file, a receiver's station). The viewer shows every station's ships together, with the station that heard each vessel last on its card and in its hover; Filter → Station looks through one station alone, and ?stations=3,5 on the viewer's requests, or /api/v1/vessels?stations=3, asks the same of the server. Statistics and plots are kept per station: with several stations, the Statistics and Plots tabs get a row of sheets with the station whose figures show at its right end, all stations added up by default. Compare on the Plots tab sets a second station, or all of them, against the one chosen, to set one station, or one decoder, against another. A station on the map opens a card of its own, as on aiscatcher.org: its ships, rate and messages, its position, the last half hour of messages and a day of activity; while the card is open the page looks through that station, and closing it goes back to what was shown before.

A message that names a station itself, as a feed from a hub does in its tag block (\s:s1001*hh\), counts at that station when stations lists it; otherwise at the input's station. So one input from a hub can serve many stations from one ship table.

A viewer whose filter names stations with id is a viewer of those stations: its station list, station cards, figures and plots show them alone, and its ships are the ones its filter lets through (see A viewer with ships of its own). Several ids, separated by commas or as a list, show those together. For example, two feeders of a hub, each on a viewer of its own, from one input:

AIS-catcher -t txt 127.0.0.1 14999 -N 8100 filter on id 1001 -N 8101 filter on id 1351

The stations themselves, with their name and position, are described in stations in a configuration file; a station that stations does not list is shown by its number, without a position, and the log says so. On a -N with such a filter, lat, lon, share_loc, use_gps and own_mmsi are left out with a note, and station is the viewer's title. The same two viewers with their stations named and placed:

{
  "config": "aiscatcher", "version": 1,
  "stations": [
    { "id": 1001, "name": "Southwood", "lat": 52.08, "lon": 4.33, "share_loc": true },
    { "id": 1351, "name": "Tyreso", "lat": 59.24, "lon": 18.24, "share_loc": true }
  ],
  "receiver": [ { "input": "rtltcp", "rtltcp": { "protocol": "txt", "host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 14999 } } ],
  "services": [
    { "port": 8100, "filter": "on", "id": [1001] },
    { "port": 8101, "filter": "on", "id": [1351] }
  ]
}

station_id on a server is refused: the error says to name the stations in the filter's id.

docs.title: A viewer with ships of its own
docs.text: A viewer with a message filter switched on (filter on with id, allow_type, block_mmsi, stations and the other terms an output takes), or that takes only some receivers (zone, groups_in), keeps a ship table of its own behind that filter, with its own history and track_time. Its file is its own backup: read at start and written as often as the station's backup says, and on exit. The places are the station's: every ship table reads the one catalogue, which places names on any viewer, this one included. Without a filter, a viewer's file, backup and history are the station's.

docs.title: HTTPS
docs.text:
A server stays on plain HTTP unless it is given a certificate you already have, as PEM files without a passphrase:

{ "server": { "port": 8443, "tls": { "cert": "fullchain.pem", "key": "privkey.pem" } } }

or on the command line:

AIS-catcher -N 8443 TLS_CERT fullchain.pem TLS_KEY privkey.pem

Relative paths are read from the configuration's folder. A renewed certificate is taken within a minute, without a restart. A file that does not load stops the start with the reason: a server never falls back to HTTP. An expired certificate still starts, with a warning in the log.

The service's user must be able to read both files. Let's Encrypt's own folder usually is closed to it, so have a renewal hook copy the files to the configuration's folder.

docs.title: Behind a reverse proxy
docs.text: A viewer treats a request from its own machine as coming from the station's owner, who may see the range figures of a station that does not share its position. A proxy on the same machine looks like that too, so it must say it is a proxy, with proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr; in nginx or the same in another proxy. Without that header everyone who reaches the proxy counts as the owner. One address may hold 32 connections, and a proxy on another machine counts as one address.

docs.title: Cross-origin access (CORS)
docs.text:
The data endpoints intended for external consumers send an Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * header so that browser-based dashboards and other web pages can fetch them directly without a proxy. The HTML pages and other resources served by the web viewer are deliberately not CORS-exposed.

CORS is enabled on:

  • /api/ships.json, /ships.json, /api/ships_full.json, /api/ships_array.json
  • /api/planes_array.json
  • /api/binmsgs.json
  • /api/history_full.json
  • /api/stat.json, /stat.json
  • /api/path.json, /api/allpath.json
  • /api/message, /api/vessel (per-vessel last message and details)
  • /api/decode (when decoder is enabled)
  • /kml (when kml is enabled)
  • /geojson and /allpath.geojson (when geojson is enabled)
  • /metrics (when prome is enabled)

The Content-Security-Policy served by the web viewer also accepts http/ws schemes in img-src and connect-src so LAN deployments work without a custom policy.

docs.title: Summary Settings
docs.text:
Server Options:

Setting (JSON key / CLI setting name) Type Default Description port integer - Single port for web server port_min integer - No longer used; a warning says so port_max integer - No longer used; a warning says so ip_bind string 0.0.0.0 The address the server listens on; every interface unless given, or this machine for a server with the API, MCP or the system service and no keys reuse_port boolean false No longer used; a warning says so zlib boolean true No longer used; a warning says so server_mode boolean false Enable hardened multi-station server mode log boolean false Show the log view in the web viewer api_v0 boolean true /ships.json, /stat.json, /api/ships.json and /api/ships_full.json as v0.70 served them; off for an entry of services unless switched on; limited does not cap them; see The ship list for scripts frame_ancestors string - CSP frame-ancestors value; set to allow embedding the viewer in an <iframe> groups_in integer all Bitmask of input groups feeding the viewer; set, the viewer keeps ships of its own from them station_id integer[] - Refused on a server: the stations a viewer shows are the ones its filter names with id; see Several stations in one viewer zone string - Comma-separated zone tags routed to this viewer; set, the viewer keeps ships of its own from them split boolean true No longer used: every station is in one view, see Several stations in one viewer Location Settings lat float - Station latitude lon float - Station longitude share_loc boolean false Share station location use_gps boolean true Use GPS data for station location own_mmsi integer - Own vessel MMSI Data Management history integer - History retention (5-43200 sec) cutoff integer - Max Distance threshold (0-10000) backup integer -1 Backup interval (5-2880 min) file string - Statistics file path stats_on_close boolean false No longer used; a warning says so realtime boolean false Enable real-time updates decoder boolean false Enable online NMEA decoder Output Formats kml boolean false Serve the ships as KML at /kml, for Google Earth geojson boolean false Serve the ships as GeoJSON at /geojson prome boolean false Serve message counts for Prometheus at /metrics; metrics says the same UI Customization message (alias msg) boolean false Store the latest decoded message per vessel, viewable via the Show Last Message item in the vessel's right-click menu station string - Station display name station_link string - Station info URL webcontrol_http string - URL for external web control endpoint context string settings Default web viewer context/tab mbtiles string - Offline map in mbtiles format mboverlay string - Offline overlay in mbtiles format fstiles string - Offline map from filesystem tile directory fsoverlay string - Offline overlay from filesystem tile directory plugin string - JavaScript plugin path style string - CSS style path plugin_dir string - Plugins directory about string - About page path. Markdown, and raw HTML in it is shown as written: use a file you trust

In addition to the options above, the web viewer accepts the standard message-filtering settings (e.g. FILTER on, allow/block by message type or channel). These restrict which messages reach this particular viewer.

docs.title: Frontend ownership
docs.text:
The viewer starts in frontend/src/bootstrap.js. It loads current server settings through features/server-config.js before importing the viewer. That module owns the configuration request, difference detection, publication and feature visibility. script.js supplies effects on the active tabs, title, selection and map. features/server-maps.js manages configured tile layers.

features/mapobjects.js adapts viewer transport and settings to frontend/shared/mapobjects.js, which owns object rendering and interaction. Binary-message settings retain their existing names; the object layer and transport use objectLayer and fetchObjects.

Managed control starts in the bundled control-app.js, whose source is frontend/control/js/app.js. It directly imports createPlaceEditor from places-editor.js and owns its instance. Places is a top-level tab without a redundant sub-tab. The shared places.js helper converts summary rows into editable GeoJSON metadata. Their CSS lives in frontend/control/css/locations.css, after the base control styles.

Vite keeps shared configuration and its preload helper outside entry chunks. Importing shared code must not import and execute a bootstrap entry point. The control bundle reuses OpenLayers; copied editor source files are excluded from the baked assets.

script.js still contains substantial legacy UI and map orchestration. Extract those by responsibility as they change; do not introduce a general framework or move everything behind one opaque controller.

docs.title: Viewer configuration ownership
docs.text:
ViewerConfiguration.h defines the shared three-stage rule: parse values and paths, prepare resources, then apply effects. Parsing opens no tile or plugin files. prepare() resolves resources before applySettings() changes databases, workers or listener options. Startup, live configuration and receiver attachment use the same effects path. configuration.values holds requested values; settings holds the effective values, including restart restrictions.

Receiver attachment reads the request and resolves its receiver zone mask. It does not overwrite effective settings. Immutable tile handles may be reused between configurations; place files reload when the configured directory changes.

The managed service loop owns configuration application and receiver attachment. HTTP handlers save files under the control file mutex, then set change flags. They do not call receiver or viewer reconfiguration while holding control locks. The loop consumes those flags and applies changes. The embedded host must also serialize its attachment calls through the viewer API.

WebViewer::state_mtx protects configuration, effective settings, receiver trackers and published frontend state. Applying changes acquires that lock, then each DB's configuration_mtx, which excludes incoming decoding while tracking configuration changes. The DB's own mtx protects ships, port membership index, history and events. DB callbacks execute under mtx: they must remain short and must not re-enter DB or acquire viewer/control locks.

Place snapshots are immutable and published by shared pointer. Control edits produce a new snapshot; the managed loop installs it in each DB, rematches stationary ships and updates the map-object sequence. Place markers use kind 10 in the delta feed. Full geometry remains available for editing and is fetched on hover for map display.

The place generation token remains in the map and vessel feeds solely to guard against matching compact place IDs from different snapshots. It no longer triggers a separate geometry download. Removing that guard would make a stale vessel feed temporarily match unrelated polygons after a reload.

Measured locally with the nationwide dataset: 470 loaded, 0 skipped, 3,143 parts, 39,050 vertices; point buffers 312,400 bytes, retained canonical definitions 1,585,322 bytes. Whole process memory was 16,285,696 bytes on this macOS build; this is not an isolated PlaceCatalogue allocation measurement or a Pi measurement.

Compatibility and review decisions:

  • Control /api/places and viewer /api/places.json return summaries. Both hosts use the version-checked /api/place.json GET for a full Feature.
  • Per-part bounds and compilation during validation were already implemented. The exact boundary check stays in the single ring pass: outer boundaries count as inside and hole boundaries as outside.
  • Voyage entries already share metadata. Keeping it preserves historical names after an area edit/deletion; an eight-byte entry cannot also retain the current timestamp and crossing coordinates.
  • The hub private PortIndex is removed. Its query adapter uses the DB index when available, and a read-only scan with its currently pinned older upstream. Updating that dependency activates the indexed path without another migration.
  • A blanket data licence and automatic shipment of mixed-source area datasets are intentionally not added without verified provenance.

Control assigns its shared area store explicitly through setPlaceCatalogue() during startup and from the managed update loop. Directory changes and disabling places replace that assignment; no viewer callback reads ControlCore on demand.

docs.title: Live viewer settings
docs.text:
Managed Control saves the normal control.viewer JSON. The viewer owner checks for changes while idle and while the receiver runs. It prepares the desired settings first, then applies them under its state lock, synchronizing with AIS input processing before changing tracking configuration or stream connections. Invalid viewer settings are rejected by Control before the configuration is saved. The HTTP listener, ships and statistics remain available; map updates do not use the old stop/reset/start cycle.

The backend has one configuration pipeline:

  1. ViewerConfiguration holds requested values and prepared resources. Its SetKey() is shared by CLI parsing, JSON loading and validation. It does not modify a live database, listener, log subscription or backup worker. Managed startup and live saves also share prepareManagedConfig(); no temporary WebViewer is constructed to validate or prepare settings.
  2. ViewerSettings.cpp owns applySettings(). Startup, live updates, receiver attachment and catalogue refresh all use this entry point. It resolves restart restrictions, computes SettingsChanges, initializes only fresh trackers, applies the effects and publishes effective frontend features.
  3. Requested values remain separate from effective values. A deferred storage change keeps its restart notice through unrelated edits and receiver restarts; it cannot silently disappear because an application overwrote the request.

The application modes express lifecycle permissions: Start activates services, Live retains receiver subscriptions, and Attach accepts the subscriptions just wired by the engine. Database allocation and backup restore happen only once; reused trackers are never initialized again. Stop only suspends workers and log subscriptions. It does not reset the configuration comparison baseline.

To add a setting, put its value/default and parser in ViewerConfiguration, then add any resource comparison to SettingsChanges and its effect to applySettings. Expose browser-facing values in FrontendConfig where necessary. Do not put runtime effects in SetKey, startServing, endAttach or the managed save path. The API lifecycle regression compares live settings, receiver restart and service restart, including retained/restored vessels and pending storage changes.

/viewer/api/config.json (or /api/config.json on a standalone viewer) returns only browser-facing settings, not the Control configuration or credentials. config_version is also included at the top level of api/ships_array.json. The managed sharing-state heartbeat also announces it, so updates reach other tabs and replay mode even when vessel polling is paused. The version is a content digest: saving identical settings does not invalidate browser caches. The browser fetches the small complete configuration document when its version changes and applies differences in place. Failed and stale responses are retried on a later vessel poll.

The bootstrap module fetches this JSON before initializing controls, with the embedded configuration as a fallback. The frontend updater handles tab visibility, station title, receiver choices, about content and server map sources. Map-source settings are JSON descriptors, rather than generated plugin code. Unchanged OpenLayers sources are retained, and existing map position and preferences survive settings updates. Place geometry keeps its own place_version and fetch path; changing an area's boundary does not download unrelated settings or reload the page.

plugin_version identifies the JavaScript and stylesheet content loaded by the page. Adding, removing or changing plugins produces a Reload prompt. Plugins are not executed a second time in the current page. Reload saves viewer preferences, map position and the selected ship. Saving configuration re-reads plugins, so a plugin file edit can be applied by saving the configuration; there is no filesystem watcher. Place files edited outside Control still require reloading the directory or restarting, as before.

Tracking storage sizing requires a service restart; receiver subscription/split changes require a receiver restart. Both are reported in restart_required and retain their effective values in the meantime. Stopping and starting reception does not discard the existing tracking database to resize it. Managed listener binding continues to belong to Control; this update path does not rebind its socket. Other engine settings still use the normal receiver restart workflow. A browser reload for plugins is separate from a receiver restart.

Validation:

  • node --test frontend/shared/test/server-config.test.js: unchanged versions, failed requests and superseded in-flight replies.

Station position changes (configuration, GPS or own-vessel reports) recalculate cached distances and bearings for existing vessels once the station has moved about 100 m from the position they were computed for; GPS jitter below that changes the reported station position only. Missing coordinates clear those values. The compact feed marks a forced refresh with full: true; clients then replace their cached fleet rather than merge it. Place catalogue changes explicitly rematch existing ships and establish fresh crossing baselines. Database reads no longer poll an area provider. Backup restores also recompute derived fields.

GeoJSON and KML capabilities are versioned with the frontend settings and their routes switch immediately. Disabling realtime also closes background streams. Backup interval changes reschedule the worker; zero disables periodic writes. An empty filename disables saving, including shutdown. A configured file is read once during startup; changing its name while running redirects future writes and never restores over live state. Shutdown still saves a nonempty filename.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: AIS-catcher is a tool for decoding and analyzing AIS signals from ships, enabling vessel movement monitoring, situational awareness, and maritime community contributions.

docs.title: Multi-Platform Support
docs.text:
• Runs on Windows, Ubuntu/Debian, Raspberry Pi, OSX, and Docker
  • Easy installation via scripts and pre-built Docker images
  • Visual Web Control interface available for Raspberry Pi and Docker deployments

docs.title: High-Performance Architecture
docs.text:
• Sensitive decoder optimized for maximum SDR performance
  • Lightweight C++ implementation for efficient resource usage
  • Neon/SSE acceleration support
  • Multi-channel decoding capability across multiple SDRs

docs.title: Flexible I/O System
docs.text:
Input Sources

  • Wide SDR hardware support (RTL-SDR, AirSpy, AirSpy HF+, HackRF, HydraSDR, SDRPlay)
  • NMEA data over network connections
  • Serial devices
  • NMEA2000 via SocketCAN

Output Options

  • NMEA format and JSON output
  • UDP/TCP/WebSocket streaming
  • HTTP push capabilities
  • MQTT broker publishing
  • Database storage (PostgreSQL)
  • OpenCPN integration
  • File-based logging

docs.title: Built-in Web Viewer
docs.text:
• Interactive map with vessel plots
  • Station dashboard
  • Message visualization graphs
  • Dark mode support
  • Mobile-friendly design
  • Extensible plugin system

docs.title: Visual Web Control Management (Raspberry Pi & Docker)
docs.text:
• Service control (start/stop)
  • Input/output configuration
  • System settings management

docs.title: PostgreSQL Features
docs.text:
• Configurable table structure
  • Vessel tracking tables
  • Message logging
  • Station metadata storage

docs.title: Multi-Channel Support
docs.text:
• Dual RTL-SDR capability
  • Multiple frequency band monitoring
  • Separate AIS channel processing
  • Performance benchmarking

docs.title: Modular Design
docs.text:
• Customizable processing pipeline
  • Experimentation-friendly architecture
  • Maintainable codebase
  • Plugin support for extended functionality

docs.title: Community Integration
docs.text:
• Data sharing via aiscatcher.org
  • Local performance tuning
  • Real-time position reports from nearby stations

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
From a receiver in its box to ships on your own map, in five steps. AIS-catcher runs in managed mode: it runs in the background, and you set it up in the dashboard in your browser.

Have these ready

Computer A Raspberry Pi, a PC or a Mac

Receiver An RTL-SDR dongle or a dAISy-catcher

Antenna A VHF antenna, tuned to 162 MHz

Not sure what to get? See What you need. Connect the antenna to the receiver, and the receiver to the computer. To run AIS-catcher with a configuration file or command-line options instead, see Manual Mode.

docs.title: Install AIS-catcher
docs.text:
Pick your computer:

Raspberry Pi and LinuxWindowsmacOSDocker

One command installs AIS-catcher and what it needs, and runs it in managed mode as a service that starts at boot:

sudo bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jvde-github/AIS-catcher/main/scripts/aiscatcher-install) -p -M"

It works on Raspberry Pi OS, Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora. See Raspberry Pi and Linux for the details.

  1. Download the Edge build from the downloads and unzip it.
  2. With an RTL-SDR, use Zadig to give it the WinUSB driver, once per dongle.
  3. Double-click start-GUI.bat in the unzipped folder.

Build it with Homebrew. This takes a few minutes:

brew install git make gcc cmake pkg-config sqlite3 librtlsdr
git clone https://github.com/jvde-github/AIS-catcher.git --depth 1
cd AIS-catcher && mkdir build && cd build
cmake .. && make && sudo make install

Then start it in managed mode:

AIS-catcher -E ~/aiscatcher.json 127.0.0.1:8118

See macOS for other receivers.

docker run --rm -it --network=host --device-cgroup-rule='c 189:* rmw' -v /dev/bus/usb:/dev/bus/usb -v ais-config:/config ghcr.io/jvde-github/ais-catcher:edge -E /config/config.json 127.0.0.1:8118

The settings live in the ais-config volume, so they survive a restart. With a dAISy-catcher, add --device /dev/ttyACM0. See Docker.

Something else, such as Android? See all installs.

docs.title: Open the dashboard
docs.text:
On the computer that runs AIS-catcher, open this address in your browser:

http://localhost:8118

From another device on your network, use that computer's name or IP address in its place, for example http://raspberrypi.local:8118. AIS-catcher then first asks you to set a password. On macOS and in Docker, the commands in the previous step only let the computer itself in: replace 127.0.0.1 with 0.0.0.0 to open the dashboard from elsewhere.

docs.title: Run the setup wizard
docs.text:
The first time, a short wizard sets up the station. Every step can be skipped, and everything can be changed later under Settings.

Welcome Press Get started.

Input Device Pick your receiver. The wizard lists the SDRs it finds on the computer, the dAISy-catcher and other serial receivers.

AIS-catcher Community To put your station on the community map, press Create station on aiscatcher.org, register it and paste the station key you get. Or press Skip.

Summary Check it, keep Start the receiver after saving ticked, and press Save & Close.

With a station key, your station gets a name, coverage statistics and its own page on aiscatcher.org. Before the summary the wizard also offers AISHub, for members of that data exchange: otherwise press Skip.

docs.title: See your ships
docs.text:
In an area with traffic, the first ships appear on the dashboard map within a few minutes. Names can take longer: ships send them less often than their position.

No ships after a few minutes?

  • Check that the antenna is connected, and that the station can see water with traffic.
  • Check that no other program uses the receiver.
  • See Troubleshooting.

Where to go next:

  • Getting Around the Dashboard: the map, the receiver controls and the settings.
  • Send Ships to Your Chart Plotter.
  • Outputs: the community map, other programs and services.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
The steps to compile AIS-catcher for RTL-SDR dongles are fairly straightforward on most systems. There are various options including a standard Makefile, a solution file for MSVC (see next section) and you can use cmake, as we will detail now.

The first step is to ensure you have the necessary dependencies and build tools installed for your device(s). For example, the following installs the minimum build tools for Ubuntu and Raspberry Pi: 

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get upgrade

sudo apt-get install git make gcc g++ cmake pkg-config libsqlite3-dev -y
For MacOS with brew installed: 
brew update
brew upgrade

brew install git make gcc cmake pkg-config sqlite3

AIS-catcher requires libraries for the particular hardware you want to use. The following table summarizes the installation instructions for all supported hardware:

System Linux/Raspberry macOS MSVC/vcpkg Command sudo apt install ... brew install ... vcpkg install ... RTL-SDR librtlsdr-dev librtlsdr rtlsdr rtlsdr:x64-windows Airspy libairspy-dev airspy - Airspy HF+ libairspyhf-dev airspyhf - HackRF libhackrf-dev hackrf - SDRplay 1A API 3.x - API 3.x SoapySDR libsoapysdr-dev - - ZeroMQ libzmq3-dev zeromq ZeroMQ ZeroMQ:x64-windows HTTP secure libssl-dev - openssl openssl:x64-windows ZIP zlib1g-dev - zlib zlib:x64-windows

Once the dependencies are in place, the process of installing AIS-catcher on Linux-based systems becomes: 

git clone https://github.com/jvde-github/AIS-catcher.git --depth 1
cd AIS-catcher
mkdir build
cd build
cmake ..
make
sudo make install
For the SDRPlay the software needs to be downloaded and installed from the website of the manufacturer. Once installed, the AIS-catcher build process automatically includes it in the build if available.

docs.title: CMake options
docs.text:
The build system exposes a number of CMake options that can be passed to cmake .. (each defaults to ON unless noted otherwise):

Option Effect -DWEBVIEWER=OFF Build a headless AIS-catcher without WebDB, WebViewer, and HTTPServer. The resulting binary is about 1.5 MB smaller; the -N flag and the server config key are gated off. Useful for backend / aggregator deployments that don't need the built-in web interface.

For example, to build a headless binary:

cmake -DWEBVIEWER=OFF ..
make

docs.title: Microsoft Visual Studio 2019+
docs.text:
Ensure that you have vcpkg installed and integrated into Visual Studio via vcpkg integrate install (as Administrator). Then install the rtl-sdr drivers as follows: 

vcpkg install rtlsdr rtlsdr:x64-windows ZeroMQ ZeroMQ:x64-windows soxr soxr:x64-windows
The included solution file in the mscv directory allows you to build AIS-catcher with RTL-SDR/ZMQ support in the Visual Studio IDE.

docs.title: Managed mode
docs.text:
AIS-catcher -E ~/aiscatcher.json 127.0.0.1:8118

Then open the dashboard in your browser, as in the Quick Start.

docs.title: Manual mode
docs.text: Start receiving with your options on the command line, for example AIS-catcher -v 10. See Manual Mode.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text: Container images are on the GitHub Container Registry: edge is the latest build of the main branch, latest the latest release. See the package page for all tags. The images do not support SDRplay devices.

docs.title: Managed mode
docs.text:
docker run --rm -it --network=host --device-cgroup-rule='c 189:* rmw' -v /dev/bus/usb:/dev/bus/usb -v ais-config:/config ghcr.io/jvde-github/ais-catcher:edge -E /config/config.json 127.0.0.1:8118
  • --device-cgroup-rule and -v /dev/bus/usb pass USB receivers through to the container, and keep them working when one is plugged in again.
  • With a dAISy-catcher or another serial receiver, add --device /dev/ttyACM0 instead.
  • The settings live in the ais-config volume, so they survive a restart.
  • To open the dashboard from another computer, replace 127.0.0.1 with 0.0.0.0. It then asks for a password.

Then open the dashboard in your browser, as in the Quick Start.

docs.title: Manual mode
docs.text:
Run the container with your AIS-catcher options at the end:

docker run --rm -it --pull always --device /dev/bus/usb ghcr.io/jvde-github/ais-catcher:latest <options>

For the web viewer (-N 8100), make its port available with -p 8100:8100, or use --network=host. See Manual Mode.

docker-shipfeeder

To feed aggregators, docker-shipfeeder from the sdr-enthusiasts community runs AIS-catcher in manual mode, with its own documentation and support.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
Pull the image again:

docker pull ghcr.io/jvde-github/ais-catcher:edge

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: On a Mac, AIS-catcher is built from source with Homebrew, so the program is made for your machine.

docs.title: Install Homebrew
docs.text:
If you don't already have Homebrew installed, you can install it by opening a terminal and running:

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

Follow the on-screen instructions to complete the installation. After installation, you may need to add Homebrew to your PATH as instructed.

docs.title: 1. Install Build Dependencies
docs.text:
First, ensure you have the necessary build tools and dependencies:

brew update
brew upgrade

brew install git make gcc cmake pkg-config sqlite3

docs.title: 2. Install SDR Hardware Libraries
docs.text:
Depending on your SDR hardware, install the appropriate drivers. For RTL-SDR dongles (most common):

brew install librtlsdr

For other hardware types, install the corresponding libraries:

Hardware Homebrew Package RTL-SDR librtlsdr Airspy airspy Airspy HF+ airspyhf HackRF hackrf ZeroMQ zeromq

For example, to install support for Airspy and HackRF:

brew install airspy hackrf

docs.title: 3. Build and Install AIS-catcher
docs.text:
Once the dependencies are in place, clone the repository and build AIS-catcher:

git clone https://github.com/jvde-github/AIS-catcher.git --depth 1
cd AIS-catcher
mkdir build
cd build
cmake ..
make
sudo make install

The build process will automatically detect and include support for any SDR libraries you have installed. You can verify the result and the features included in your build with AIS-catcher -L.

Note

Building from source can take several minutes depending on your Mac's specifications. The executable will be optimized for your specific hardware.

docs.title: Managed mode
docs.text:
Start AIS-catcher with the dashboard:

AIS-catcher -E ~/aiscatcher.json 127.0.0.1:8118

Then open the dashboard in your browser, as in the Quick Start. To open it from another computer, replace 127.0.0.1 with 0.0.0.0. It then asks for a password.

docs.title: Manual mode
docs.text:
Start receiving with your options on the command line, for example:

AIS-catcher -v 10

See Manual Mode.

docs.title: Start at Login
docs.text: Unlike the Linux/Raspberry Pi version, there is no automated background service setup script for macOS. However, you can create a launch agent to run AIS-catcher automatically at startup using launchd.

docs.title: Creating a Launch Agent
docs.text:
1. First, verify the installation path of AIS-catcher:
which AIS-catcher

This will return either /usr/local/bin/AIS-catcher (Intel Macs) or /opt/homebrew/bin/AIS-catcher (Apple Silicon Macs). Use this path in the next step.

  1. Create a launch agent plist file (note: do not use sudo for this):
nano ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.aiscatcher.plist
  1. Add the following content, adjusting the path and parameters for your setup:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>Label</key>
    <string>com.aiscatcher</string>
    <key>ProgramArguments</key>
    <array>
        <string>/usr/local/bin/AIS-catcher</string>
        <string>-v</string>
        <!-- Add additional parameters as separate strings, for example: -->
        <!-- <string>-u</string> -->
        <!-- <string>5.9.207.224</string> -->
        <!-- <string>2947</string> -->
    </array>
    <key>RunAtLoad</key>
    <true/>
    <key>KeepAlive</key>
    <true/>
    <key>StandardOutPath</key>
    <string>/Users/YOUR_USERNAME/aiscatcher.log</string>
    <key>StandardErrorPath</key>
    <string>/Users/YOUR_USERNAME/aiscatcher.error.log</string>
</dict>
</plist>

Important Notes: - Replace /usr/local/bin/AIS-catcher with the path from step 1 if different (e.g., /opt/homebrew/bin/AIS-catcher for Apple Silicon) - Replace YOUR_USERNAME with your actual macOS username - Each command-line argument must be in its own <string> tag (e.g., -u, 5.9.207.224, and 2947 as three separate strings) - Logs are stored in your home directory to persist across reboots (unlike /tmp which is cleared on restart)

  1. Load the launch agent:
launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.aiscatcher.plist
  1. To start the service immediately:
launchctl start com.aiscatcher
  1. To stop the service:
launchctl stop com.aiscatcher
  1. To unload the service (if you need to make changes to the plist):
launchctl unload ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.aiscatcher.plist

docs.title: Updating AIS-catcher
docs.text:
To update to the latest version, navigate to your AIS-catcher directory and rebuild:

cd AIS-catcher
git pull
cd build
cmake ..
make
sudo make install

docs.title: Command Not Found
docs.text:
If you get a "command not found" error after installation, ensure /usr/local/bin is in your PATH. Add this to your ~/.zshrc or ~/.bash_profile:

export PATH="/usr/local/bin:$PATH"

docs.title: CMake Not Found
docs.text: If cmake is not found, ensure Homebrew is properly installed and in your PATH. After installing Homebrew, you may need to run the commands shown at the end of the Homebrew installation.

docs.title: Missing Libraries
docs.text: If the build fails due to missing libraries, make sure you've installed the required SDR libraries with Homebrew as described in step 2.

docs.title: Alternative: MacPorts
docs.text: While this guide focuses on Homebrew, AIS-catcher can also be built using MacPorts. The following instructions were contributed by the community (credit: GitHub Discussion #500).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
First, install Xcode command line tools:

xcode-select --install

Download and install MacPorts from macports.org/install.php, choosing the version specific to your macOS release.

docs.title: Installation Steps
docs.text:
1. Install base prerequisites via MacPorts:
sudo port install git make gcc cmake sqlite3
  1. Install your SDR device driver. For RTL-SDR dongles:
sudo port install rtl-sdr

For other hardware, install the corresponding MacPorts package.

  1. Download, build, and install AIS-catcher:
cd
git clone https://github.com/jvde-github/AIS-catcher.git --depth 1
cd ~/AIS-catcher
mkdir ~/AIS-catcher/build
cd ~/AIS-catcher/build
cmake ..
make
sudo make install

After installation, verify it works by running:

AIS-catcher -L

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Pick your system. Each page shows the install for managed mode and for manual mode.

Popular Raspberry Pi and Linux One-line install script for Raspberry Pi OS, Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora, runs as a background service Windows Pre-built binaries — unzip and double-click Docker Pre-built container images from the GitHub registry macOS Build with Homebrew, optimized for your Mac Android Run AIS-catcher on an Android phone or tablet, from its GitHub page Build from Source Compile AIS-catcher yourself on any platform

docs.title: Raspberry Pi and Linux
docs.text: One script installs AIS-catcher and what it needs, and sets it up as a service that starts at boot. It works on Raspberry Pi OS, Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora. If curl is missing, install it first with sudo apt install curl (or sudo dnf install curl on Fedora).

docs.title: Managed mode
docs.text:
sudo bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jvde-github/AIS-catcher/main/scripts/aiscatcher-install) -p -M"

Then open the dashboard in your browser, as in the Quick Start.

Coming from manual mode?

Managed mode starts with fresh settings: your /etc/AIS-catcher/config.json and config.cmd are not carried over. The files stay where they are, so you can look at them while you set up the station in the dashboard. Running the installer again on a managed station is an update, and keeps your settings.

docs.title: Manual mode
docs.text:
sudo bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jvde-github/AIS-catcher/main/scripts/aiscatcher-install) -p"

The service then runs the settings in /etc/AIS-catcher. See Running as a Service.

docs.title: Pre-built or from source
docs.text:
The -p option installs a pre-built package: a .deb on Debian, Ubuntu and Raspberry Pi OS, or an .rpm on Fedora 43 and 44 (x86_64 and aarch64). Leave out -p to build AIS-catcher from source instead, for example in managed mode:

sudo bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jvde-github/AIS-catcher/main/scripts/aiscatcher-install) -M"

A build takes about 20 minutes on a Raspberry Pi 4, and is needed on other Fedora releases and for PostgreSQL support.

Note

The pre-built packages do not run on the first Raspberry Pi and the first Pi Zero.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text: Run the same install command again. Your settings are kept.

docs.title: AIS-catcher-control
docs.text:
AIS-catcher-control is a separate tool to start and stop AIS-catcher, read its log, update it and reboot the computer from the browser. Install it with:

sudo bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jvde-github/AIS-catcher-control/main/install_ais_catcher_control.sh)"

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: AIS-catcher for Windows is a ZIP file: download it from the downloads below and unzip it to a folder. Take the Edge build.

docs.title: Managed mode
docs.text:
1. With an RTL-SDR, use Zadig to give it the WinUSB driver, once per dongle.
  2. Double-click start-GUI.bat in the unzipped folder.
  3. Open the dashboard in your browser, as in the Quick Start.

docs.title: Manual mode
docs.text:
Run AIS-catcher.exe from a command prompt in the unzipped folder, or put your options in start.bat with Notepad and double-click it. See Manual Mode.

Does not start?

Install the Microsoft Visual C++ runtime. It is usually already there.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
The AIS-catcher executables are built with the latest Windows MSVC compiler. Please update your libraries before starting the executables below. Issues have been reported on Windows 10.

Version Win32 x64 Win32 + SDRPlay x64 + SDRPlay Edge (latest, recommended) ZIP ZIP not shipped not shipped v0.71 (latest release) ZIP ZIP not shipped not shipped v0.70 (older, no managed mode) ZIP ZIP ZIP ZIP

Edge is the latest build, not the browser

Edge is the latest build of AIS-catcher, produced automatically from the main branch each time the code changes. It is the recommended download. Managed mode and start-GUI.bat are in Edge and in v0.71. The name refers to the build, not the Microsoft Edge browser.

v0.70 is an older release, kept for its SDRPlay builds (see below). It predates managed mode, so started with -E it stops with Option -E is obsolete.

SDRPlay builds for Windows

v0.70 is the last Windows release with SDRPlay support. The SDRPlay API installer can no longer be downloaded from an automated build, so these binaries are no longer produced. The v0.70 downloads above remain available.

SDRPlay support itself has not been removed: it is still part of AIS-catcher and is available on Linux and macOS, where the API is installed separately. On Windows you can still build from source after installing the SDRPlay API yourself.

docs.title: Ask Your Station, the API
docs.text:
Your station answers questions over HTTP: the vessels it hears, their tracks, port calls and events, as JSON. Any program that can fetch a web address can read them.

You need: AIS-catcher receiving ships.

docs.title: Switch the API on
docs.text:
In the dashboard, open Settings → Services → Main. Main is the server that serves the dashboard's map, on the port after the dashboard's: 8119 unless you changed it.

Under Serves, switch API on and press Save changes. The server serves it at once.

Dashboard open to your network?

Then Main is too, and its Access section asks who may read the API. Press New key to make a key, or choose Open to let everyone on the network read it.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: At the top of Main's page, press Try the API. Pick an Endpoint, such as /api/v1/vessels, and press Send. The answer appears below it, with the curl line that repeats the request.

docs.title: Ask from a program
docs.text:
On the computer that runs AIS-catcher, send the same request from a terminal:

curl "http://127.0.0.1:8119/api/v1/vessels?limit=10"

The answer is {"data": [ ... ], "meta": { ... }}, with one vessel in each row of data.

docs.title: Reach it from another computer
docs.text:
To let programs on other computers ask, give them a server of their own. Under Settings → Services, press + Add server. The new server has the API switched on and its own Port.

Set Listens on to Network. Under Access, keep Keys and press New key. Name the key, press Make key and copy it: it is shown once. Then press Save changes.

A program sends the key with every request, to the server's own port:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://station.local:8110/api/v1/vessels?limit=10"

docs.title: What next
docs.text:
• API explains the lists, the filters and the keys. The API reference lists every route and field.
  • Let an AI Assistant Read Your Station offers the same data to an assistant.

docs.title: In manual mode
docs.text: In a configuration file, "api": true switches the API on for a server of the services list. On the command line, api on after -N does the same. See API.

docs.title: Let an AI Assistant Read Your Station
docs.text:
With MCP switched on, an AI assistant can ask your station questions: which ships are near, who arrived today, whether the station is healthy. The assistant only reads. It cannot change the station.

You need: AIS-catcher receiving ships, and an assistant that speaks MCP over HTTP, such as Claude Code.

docs.title: Switch MCP on
docs.text:
In the dashboard, open Settings → Services → Main. Under Serves, switch MCP on. Switch System on too if the assistant should also see the station's health, its receivers and the log.

Press Save changes. The server serves it at once.

Dashboard open to your network?

Then Main is too, and its Access section asks who may read it. Press New key to make a key. System is never open on the network: it always takes a key.

docs.title: Try a tool
docs.text: At the top of Main's page, press Try the API and choose MCP. Pick a Tool, such as search_vessels, and press Call. The answer is what the assistant gets.

docs.title: Connect the assistant
docs.text:
Under Connect an assistant, press Copy and run the line where your assistant runs. For Claude Code on the computer that runs AIS-catcher, it reads:

claude mcp add --transport http aiscatcher http://127.0.0.1:8119/mcp

Other assistants that speak MCP over HTTP take the same address.

docs.title: From another computer
docs.text:
An assistant on another computer needs a server that listens on the network and takes keys. Add one as in Ask Your Station, the API, and switch MCP on for it.

In Try the API, pick that server under Server and enter its key under Key. The line under Connect an assistant then names the server's address and adds the header for the key.

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
Ask your assistant: Which vessels did my station hear in the last hour? It answers with ships from your own station.

MCP: an assistant reads the station lists every tool, and says how much room a model on your own computer needs for them.

docs.title: In manual mode
docs.text: In a configuration file, "mcp": true switches MCP on for a server of the services list. On the command line, mcp on after -N does the same. See MCP: an assistant reads the station.

docs.title: Send Ships to Your Chart Plotter
docs.text:
AIS-catcher can pass every message it receives on to OpenCPN, a chart plotter or a navigation app on your network, as NMEA over UDP. The ships then appear on that program's chart.

You need: AIS-catcher receiving ships, and the address of the computer or plotter that should get them. Port 10110 is the usual port for AIS.

On the same computer?

If the chart plotter runs on the same computer as AIS-catcher, use the address 127.0.0.1.

docs.title: Add a UDP output
docs.text: In the dashboard, open Settings, choose Outputs and press + Add output. Pick UDP.

docs.title: Enter the address
docs.text: Give the output a Name, such as Chart plotter. Enter the Address and Port of the program that receives it.

docs.title: Save
docs.text: Press Save changes. The output starts sending at once.

docs.title: Set up the chart plotter
docs.text: Tell the receiving program to listen for NMEA over UDP on the same port. In OpenCPN: Options → Connections → Add Connection, choose Network, protocol UDP, port 10110, and data protocol NMEA 0183.

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
• The ships appear on the plotter's chart within a minute. Names can take a few minutes longer: ships send them less often than their position.

  • In the dashboard, open Statistics. Under Data Throughput, the output's Bytes out keeps growing.

No ships on the plotter?

  • Bytes out grows: AIS-catcher is sending. Check the port in the plotter and the firewall on that computer. UDP gets no reply, so AIS-catcher cannot tell whether anything is listening.
  • Dropped grows instead: AIS-catcher cannot send to that address. Check the address, and that both machines are on the same network.

docs.title: More
docs.text:
• Several programs: add an output for each one.
  • Every device on the network: enter the network's broadcast address, for example 192.168.1.255, and switch on Broadcast under Options.
  • Programs that connect in: some programs want to connect to AIS-catcher themselves. Add a TCP Server output for those instead.

docs.title: Share with the Community Map
docs.text:
AIS-catcher can add the ships you receive to the live map at aiscatcher.org. A new station shares from the start, anonymously. A free station key gives it a name, coverage statistics and its own page.

You need: AIS-catcher receiving ships.

docs.title: Open the community map page
docs.text: In the dashboard, open Settings, choose Outputs and then Community map.

docs.title: Switch sharing on
docs.text:
Check that Share with the Community Map is on. Without a key the station is anonymous, and the page says so.

Without a key, the community map takes radio inputs only. A serial receiver or a network input is shared once the station has a key.

docs.title: Get a station key
docs.text: This step is optional. Press Get a key: it opens aiscatcher.org, where you register the station and get its key. Paste the key in Sharing Key.

docs.title: Save
docs.text: Press Save changes. Once a key is in, the button next to it reads Edit station details and opens your station on aiscatcher.org.

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
• Within a few minutes your ships show on the live map.
  • With a key, your station has its own page under Stations.
  • The community map icon in the dashboard's control bar shows whether the station shares.

To stop sharing, switch Share with the Community Map off and save. Nothing then leaves the station.

docs.title: In manual mode
docs.text: On the command line, -X switches sharing on, with the station key after it. In a configuration file the keys are sharing and sharing_key. See Community Feed.

docs.title: Getting Around the Dashboard
docs.text: In managed mode, AIS-catcher runs in the background and you set it up in the dashboard, in your browser. Open port 8118 of the computer that runs it, for example http://localhost:8118. The Quick Start covers the first start and the setup wizard.

docs.title: The Map
docs.text:
The map fills the dashboard and shows the ships your station receives, live. Its menus at the top open the ship list, statistics and the map's own settings.

This map loads no plugins and no about page, and it has no log tab: the dashboard keeps the log under Settings → System → Log. For a map with plugins or an about page, add a server under Settings → Services and open that map instead.

docs.title: The Control Bar
docs.text:
The bar at the bottom runs the station:

  • A B C D: a light for each AIS channel, which flashes as messages arrive.
  • Start or Stop: starts and stops the receiver.
  • Settings: opens the settings.
  • Running or Stopped, with the time since the start. A count of warnings and errors appears next to it; press it to open the log.
  • The community map icon, on the right: its colour shows whether the station shares with the community map. It links to aiscatcher.org.
  • The arrow on the left hides the bar. Controls brings it back.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Settings opens a list on the left. Each item opens a page:

Item What it holds Stations Your station's name and position. Inputs Your receivers. See Receiver. Outputs The community map and the programs that get your data. See Outputs. Flow Which input reaches which output. Services The map servers, Home Assistant and webhooks. Places Ports, berths, anchorages and zones on the map. See Places. System Status, Data & history, Log, Config file, Access and About.

Each page ends with Cancel and Save changes. A saved change is used at once; the receiver restarts by itself when a change needs it.

Under System:

  • Status shows the receiver and the computer. Copy for bug report copies both.
  • Data & history sets whether ships and statistics are kept over a restart.
  • Config file shows the file the dashboard writes.
  • Access sets the password and HTTPS. See Remote Access and Security.
  • About has Run setup, which runs the setup wizard again.

docs.title: Places
docs.text:
Settings → Places is an editor for the places on the map: ports, berths, anchorages, terminals, guard zones and more. The first time, it asks to enable places and shows the folder they are saved in. Press Save and continue.

Pick a place from the list or on the map, or press New place. Draw or reshape its outline, set its Type and its Parent, and press Save place. A save takes effect at once, on the map and for every ship inside the changed outline.

  • Import…, in the place menu, takes a GeoJSON Feature from anywhere. What it recognises is carried over: the name, the type, codes, the parent, category and rank. Everything else in the file is kept, and a Feature that says nothing about itself becomes a guard zone. The result opens for review and is stored when you save.
  • Import shape and Paste shape, in the map's toolbar, replace only the outline of the place you are editing.

To use a folder of place files instead, enter it under System → Data & history → Files → Place directory.

docs.title: Starting Managed Mode Yourself
docs.text:
The installs start AIS-catcher in managed mode for you. Started by hand, it takes -E with its configuration file and the address the dashboard listens on:

AIS-catcher -E ~/aiscatcher.json 127.0.0.1:8118

With 127.0.0.1, only this computer can open the dashboard. See Remote Access and Security to open it to your network.

Prefer a configuration file or the command line? See Manual Mode.

docs.title: Vessels in Home Assistant
docs.text:
AIS-catcher can publish your station and the vessels you follow to Home Assistant over MQTT. With discovery on, Home Assistant adds them as entities by itself.

You need: Home Assistant with its MQTT integration set up, and the address of the MQTT broker it uses, with the user and password if it asks for them.

docs.title: Open the Home Assistant page
docs.text: In the dashboard, open Settings, choose Services and then Home Assistant.

docs.title: Enter the broker
docs.text: Enter the Broker, for example mqtt://homeassistant.local:1883. Fill in User and Password if the broker asks for them.

docs.title: Choose the vessels to follow
docs.text: Leave Home Assistant discovery on. Under Watched vessels, enter the MMSI of each vessel you want to follow, one per line. Each one becomes a device tracker in Home Assistant.

docs.title: Save
docs.text: Press Save changes.

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
In Home Assistant, open Settings → Devices & services → MQTT. It lists an AIS-catcher device with your station's entities, such as Vessels, Message rate and Range of the last 24 hours, and a device tracker for each watched vessel.

Home Assistant and MQTT state lists every topic and entity.

docs.title: In manual mode
