docs.text: In a configuration file, the section is mqtt_state. On the command line, -W takes the broker's address and the same keys. See Home Assistant and MQTT state; to post events to Home Assistant without MQTT, see Webhooks.

docs.title: Receiver
docs.text:
Settings → Inputs lists your receivers. Each one has its own page. The setup wizard adds the first one; + Add input adds another.

  • Device Type: the kind of receiver: RTL-SDR, Airspy, HackRF, SDRplay and the other SDRs, Serial (NMEA receiver), UDP (NMEA over the network), a Network client or SpyServer. A dAISy-catcher is a Serial (NMEA receiver) input; the setup wizard fills in its settings for you.
  • Find devices looks for receivers on this computer. Pick one to fill in its details.
  • Serial Key picks one dongle by its serial number, when more than one is plugged in. With a single dongle, leave it empty.
  • Active switches the input on or off without deleting it. A hollow dot in the list marks an input that is off.
  • Station is where this antenna stands, from the stations under Settings → Stations.
  • Advanced settings holds the rest, such as the tuner gain, the sample rate, the frequency correction and the decoding engine.
  • Docs opens the reference for that kind of receiver.

Press Save changes: the change is used at once, and the receiver restarts by itself when the change needs it.

A mark next to an input in the list means it needs attention: hover over it to see why, for example a device that is unplugged or used by another program.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Settings → Outputs lists where your data goes: the community map first, then the outputs you added.

docs.title: Community Map
docs.text:
Share with the Community Map sends your ships to the aiscatcher.org community map. A new station shares from the start, anonymously.

To give your station a name, coverage statistics and its own page, register it:

  1. Create a station on aiscatcher.org. You get a station key.
  2. Paste the key in Sharing Key and press Save changes.

Once a key is in, the button next to it reads Edit station details and opens your station on aiscatcher.org. Switch sharing off and nothing leaves the station.

The community map icon in the control bar shows the state at a glance.

docs.title: Other Programs
docs.text:
+ Add output opens Add an output:

Output What it does UDP NMEA to another program on the network HTTP Post batches to a web address MQTT Publish to a broker TCP Client Connect out to a server and send TCP Server Let programs connect in and read Database SQLite, PostgreSQL or CSV files Screen Print the messages in the log

Fill in what the output needs, such as an address and a port, and give it a Name. The rest is under Advanced settings. Active switches an output off without deleting it.

Send Ships to Your Chart Plotter walks through a UDP output, start to finish.

A mark next to an output in the list means it needs attention: amber for a setting, red for a problem while it runs. Hover over it to see why.

docs.title: Maps, Home Assistant and Webhooks
docs.text:
These are under Settings → Services. + Add server adds a map of its own on another port, which you can share on your network or publicly, with the API and other feeds beside it. Home Assistant and Webhooks have their own pages there.

Press Save changes: the change is used at once.

docs.title: Connect Your Receivers
docs.text:
Each input is a receiver that AIS comes from: an RTL-SDR or another radio, a dAISy-catcher on a serial port, or NMEA that arrives over the network. Add an input for every receiver you have.

You need: each receiver plugged into the computer that runs AIS-catcher. For NMEA over the network, the port it arrives on.

docs.title: Add an input
docs.text: In the dashboard, open Settings, choose Inputs and press + Add input. The setup wizard adds the first receiver; + Add input adds another.

docs.title: Pick the receiver
docs.text:
Press Find devices and pick the receiver from the list. This fills in its Device Type and its Serial Key, the serial number that tells two dongles apart.

For a receiver that is not in the list, choose the Device Type yourself. A dAISy-catcher is a Serial (NMEA receiver): press Find ports to pick its port.

docs.title: Name it
docs.text: Give the input a Name, such as Mast dongle. With more than one receiver, Statistics lists each by its name.

docs.title: Choose its station
docs.text: Under Station, choose where this antenna stands. With one station, leave it as it is. For an antenna at another place, pick New station… in the list.

docs.title: Save and start
docs.text: Press Save changes. If the receiver is stopped, press Start in the control bar.

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
• In an area with traffic, the ships the new receiver hears appear on the dashboard map within a few minutes.
  • In the dashboard, open Statistics. Under System, each input is listed as a Device, and Message rate shows what comes in.

Nothing from the new receiver?

Open Settings → Inputs. A mark next to an input means it needs attention: hover over it to see why, for example a device that is unplugged or used by another program. A hollow dot marks an input that is switched off.

docs.title: In manual mode
docs.text: In a configuration file, each receiver is an entry of the receiver list: see Receivers. Input Configuration covers the command line and has a page for every kind of device.

docs.title: Remote Access and Security
docs.text:
By default the dashboard is only reachable from the machine AIS-catcher runs on (127.0.0.1). To administer it from another machine on your network, bind to all interfaces:

AIS-catcher -E /etc/AIS-catcher/config.json 0.0.0.0:8118

When bound to anything other than 127.0.0.1/localhost, a password is required: on first access the dashboard asks you to set one, and every subsequent session requires logging in.

Warning

The dashboard is intended for use on your local network. If you want to expose your station's data publicly, do not expose the dashboard — share your data via the community feed or add a web viewer instead.

docs.title: HTTPS for the dashboard
docs.text:
The password travels over this connection, so give the dashboard HTTPS when it is reached over a network. You need a certificate as PEM files without a passphrase, readable by the service's user.

  • In the dashboard: Settings → System → Access. Enter the two files, which must be in the configuration's folder, and press Apply HTTPS. The files are checked first, the dashboard moves to https:// at once and asks for the password again. Leave both empty to go back to plain HTTP.

  • On the command line: for that run only, not saved in the file.

    AIS-catcher -E /etc/AIS-catcher/aiscatcher.json 0.0.0.0:8118 TLS_CERT fullchain.pem TLS_KEY privkey.pem

  • In the configuration file: "control": { "tls": { "cert": "fullchain.pem", "key": "privkey.pem" } }.

A renewed certificate is taken within a minute. The dashboard answers on one scheme only and never falls back to HTTP. If the files stop loading, the Access page says why; if they do not load at start, AIS-catcher stops with the reason in the log until they are fixed, or tls is taken out of the file. The map's own port has its own HTTPS setting, under Services.

docs.title: Name and Place Your Station
docs.text:
Tell AIS-catcher where your antenna stands. Every ship's distance and bearing, and your station's range, are measured from there.

You need: the position of your antenna, as a latitude and longitude or as a spot you can find on a map.

docs.title: Open your station
docs.text:
In the dashboard, open Settings and choose Stations. Your station comes first: every input stands there until you add more stations.

Give it a Name, such as Harbour mast.

docs.title: Set the position
docs.text: Under Position, switch No position off if it is on. Type the Latitude and Longitude in decimal degrees, or press Pick on map and click where the antenna stands. Antenna height (m) is optional.

docs.title: A station that moves
docs.text:
On land, skip this step. On a boat, the position you typed is where the station stands until something moves it:

  • Follow GPS moves the station with each fix from a GPS, or from an AIS receiver that passes GPS sentences.
  • Rides a vessel (MMSI) takes the MMSI of the ship the station is on. The station is then wherever that ship last reported.

docs.title: Save
docs.text: Press Save changes. The station uses the new position at once.

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
• The dashboard map shows the station where you put it.
  • Click a ship: its card shows the Distance and Bearing from the station.
  • In the dashboard, open Statistics. Under This Session, Max Distance is the furthest ship heard since the start.

No distance or bearing?

A map shows them only when its server shows where the stations are. Open Settings → Services → Main and, under Shows, switch Station locations on. On a new installation it is on already.

docs.title: In manual mode
docs.text: In a configuration file, a station is an entry of the stations list: see Stations. On the command line, the web viewer's lat and lon place the station: see Web Viewer.

docs.title: JSON Format
docs.text:
Below documents the JSON format used for decoding AIS messages. Depending on the settings for JSON decoding fields may or may not be included in the outcome. With format JSON_NMEA only the common fields will be included in the JSON package. The AIS message details are still included in the NMEA array embedded in the JSON. With format JSON_FULL the program will perform a full decoding of the AIS messages and include in the JSON. The output format is largely compatible with gpsdecode. JSON_SPARSE writes the same decode with a reduced key dictionary, and JSON_ANNOTATED wraps each value as an object with value plus the unit, description and lookup text of the key where defined.

Not-available values. A field whose wire value is the standard's "not available" code is omitted from the JSON rather than emitted as a sentinel: position 181°/91°, speed 102.3 kn, course 360°, heading 511, second 60, ETA month/day 0 and hour 24/minute 60, IMO 0, draught 0, and the equivalent codes in binary application messages. The tables name the sentinel where it matters. Two fields keep the raw code: turn_unscaled and the type 5 eta string.

docs.title: Message types index
docs.text:
Position reports 1, 2, 3 — Class A · 4 — Base Station · 9 — SAR Aircraft · 11 — UTC Response · 18 — Class B · 19 — Extended Class B · 27 — Long-Range

Static / voyage 5 — Static and Voyage · 24 — Static Data Report

Binary / safety / text 6 — Binary Addressed · 7, 13 — Binary / Safety Ack · 8 — Binary Broadcast · 12 — Safety Addressed · 14 — Safety Broadcast · 25, 26 — Single/Multi Slot Binary

Network management 10 — UTC Inquiry · 15 — Interrogation · 16 — Assignment Mode · 17 — DGNSS · 20 — Data Link Mgmt · 22 — Channel Mgmt · 23 — Group Assignment

Aids to navigation 21 — Aid-to-Nav Report · 28 — AtoN Report (single-slot)

Other Common fields · ASM payloads (Type 6 / 8) · Notes

docs.title: Common Fields
docs.text:
These fields are present in every emitted message:

Field Type Description Example class String Always "AIS" "AIS" device String Always "AIS-catcher" "AIS-catcher" version Integer AIS-catcher version number that produced this output 70 driver Integer Numeric device driver identifier 3 hardware String Hardware/device product name reported by the driver "RTL-SDR" scaled Boolean Values scaled to engineering units true channel String VHF channel (A or B) "A" nmea Array of String Original NMEA sentence(s) ["!AIVDM,1,1,,A,13...,0*5C"] type Integer AIS message type number (1–28) 1 repeat Integer Repeat indicator (0..3; 3 = do not repeat) 0 mmsi Integer MMSI number 123456789

Optional fields, added depending on input mode and message contents:

Field Type Unit Description rxtime String UTC Host receive time (YYYYMMDDHHMMSS), always set from the local clock when AIS-catcher decoded the message. Added when timestamping is enabled (-M T). rxuxtime Float seconds Same instant as rxtime, expressed as Unix epoch with microsecond fraction. Added with rxtime. signalpower Float dB Signal power level. Added when stats are enabled (-M D). ppm Float ppm Estimated frequency offset of the receiver during decoding. Added with signalpower. toa Float seconds Upstream time of arrival, if the input carried one. For JSON input that is the source's toa or rxuxtime field (toa wins when both are present); for NMEA it is the tag-block c: timestamp. Omitted when the input had no upstream time. station_id Integer or String – Station identifier (numeric, or 7-char ASCII for SLS). quality Integer – Quality flags, present only when non-zero. Error flags: checksum 0x0200, undersized 0x0400, oversized 0x0800. Bits 0–5 carry reception-quality marks (plausible, confirmed, suspect, duplicate, echo, late, dense). A flagged message is still forwarded to every output unless that output's filter is on (FILTER on, default exclusions undersized,checksum). country String – Flag country name derived from MMSI MID. Added with -M M. country_code String – ISO-3166 alpha-2 country code derived from MMSI MID. Added with -M M.

docs.title: Type 1, 2, 3: Position Report Class A
docs.text: Field Type Range/Units Description status Integer 0–15 Navigation status status_text String See note 1 Navigation status description turn Integer ±720 °/min Rate of turn (scaled, °/min). Omitted when not available (raw -128); ±127 = turning right/left at more than 5°/30 s without a turn indicator turn_unscaled Integer -128..127 Raw ROT field, always present (-128 = not available) speed Float 0–102.2 knots Speed over ground; omitted when not available (102.3) accuracy Boolean – Position accuracy flag (1 = DGPS <10 m) lon Float ±180° Longitude; omitted when not available (181°) lat Float ±90° Latitude; omitted when not available (91°) course Float 0–359.9° Course over ground; omitted when not available (360) heading Integer 0–359° True heading; omitted when not available (511) second Integer 0–59, 61–63 UTC second; omitted when not available (60); 61 = manual input, 62 = dead reckoning, 63 = positioning system inoperative maneuver Integer 0–2 Maneuver indicator power Boolean – Transmit power flag (M.1371-6 Table 46; 0 = high, 1 = low). Was part of spare in pre-M.1371-6 revisions. raim Boolean – RAIM flag radio Integer – Radio status (19-bit SOTDMA/ITDMA state). When non-zero, sub-fields are also decoded — see note 5.

docs.title: Type 4, 11: Base Station Report / UTC Date Response
docs.text: Field Type Range Description timestamp String ISO-8601 UTC timestamp (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ) year Integer YYYY UTC year; omitted when not available (0) month Integer 1–12 UTC month; omitted when not available (0) day Integer 1–31 UTC day; omitted when not available (0) hour Integer 0–23 UTC hour; omitted when not available (24) minute Integer 0–59 UTC minute; omitted when not available (60) second Integer 0–59 UTC second; omitted when not available (60) accuracy Boolean – Position accuracy flag lon Float ±180° Longitude; omitted when not available (181°) lat Float ±90° Latitude; omitted when not available (91°) epfd Integer 0–8 EPFD type epfd_text String See note 2 EPFD description transmission_control Boolean – Transmission control for satellite broadcast (M.1371-6 Table 49; 0 = stop msg 27 within base coverage, 1 = transmit msg 27). Was part of spare in pre-M.1371-6 revisions. raim Boolean – RAIM flag radio Integer – Radio status. See note 5 for sub-fields.

docs.title: Type 5: Static and Voyage Related Data
docs.text: Field Type Range Description ais_version Integer 0–3 AIS version imo Integer 1–999999999 IMO number; omitted when not available (0) callsign String 7 chars Radio callsign shipname String 20 chars Vessel name shiptype Integer 0–99 Ship type code shiptype_text String See note 3 Ship type description to_bow Integer 0–511 m Dimension to bow to_stern Integer 0–511 m Dimension to stern to_port Integer 0–63 m Dimension to port to_starboard Integer 0–63 m Dimension to starboard epfd Integer 0–8 EPFD type epfd_text String See note 2 EPFD description eta String MM-DDTHH:MMZ Estimated time of arrival (UTC), always present; 00-00T24:60Z when not available month Integer 1–12 ETA month (also exposed individually); omitted when not available (0) day Integer 1–31 ETA day; omitted when not available (0) hour Integer 0–23 ETA hour; omitted when not available (24) minute Integer 0–59 ETA minute; omitted when not available (60) draught Float 0–25.5 m Draught in metres; omitted when not available (0) destination String 20 chars Destination port dte Boolean – Data terminal equipment ready (0 = ready)

docs.title: Type 6: Binary Addressed Message
docs.text:
Field Type Range Description seqno Integer 0–3 Sequence number dest_mmsi Integer 9 digits Destination MMSI retransmit Boolean – Retransmit flag dac Integer – Designated Area Code fid Integer – Functional Identifier data String hex Raw binary payload (only when no decoder matched)

When the (DAC, FID) pair is recognised, the payload is decoded into structured fields instead of data — see ASM payloads (Type 6 / Type 8) below.

docs.title: Type 7, 13: Binary / Safety Acknowledge
docs.text: Field Type Range Description mmsi1 Integer 9 digits MMSI number 1 mmsiseq1 Integer 0–3 Sequence for MMSI 1 mmsi2 Integer 9 digits MMSI number 2 (if present) mmsiseq2 Integer 0–3 Sequence for MMSI 2 mmsi3 Integer 9 digits MMSI number 3 (if present) mmsiseq3 Integer 0–3 Sequence for MMSI 3 mmsi4 Integer 9 digits MMSI number 4 (if present) mmsiseq4 Integer 0–3 Sequence for MMSI 4

docs.text:
Field Type Range Description dac Integer – Designated Area Code fid Integer – Functional Identifier data String hex Raw binary payload (only when no decoder matched)

When the (DAC, FID) pair is recognised, the payload is decoded into structured fields — see ASM payloads (Type 6 / Type 8) below.

docs.title: Type 9: Standard SAR Aircraft Position Report
docs.text: Field Type Range Description alt Integer 0–4094 m Altitude; omitted when not available (4095) speed Integer 0–1022 knots Speed over ground; omitted when not available (1023) accuracy Boolean – Position accuracy lon Float ±180° Longitude; omitted when not available (181°) lat Float ±90° Latitude; omitted when not available (91°) course Float 0–359.9° Course over ground; omitted when not available (360) second Integer 0–59 UTC second; omitted when not available (60) alt_sensor Boolean – Altitude sensor (M.1371-6 Table 57; 0 = GNSS, 1 = barometric). Was part of regional in pre-M.1371-6 revisions. dte Boolean – DTE flag assigned Boolean – Assigned mode flag raim Boolean – RAIM flag radio Integer – Radio status. See note 5 for sub-fields.

docs.title: Type 10: UTC/Date Inquiry
docs.text: Field Type Range Description dest_mmsi Integer 9 digits Destination MMSI

docs.title: Type 11: UTC/Date Response
docs.text: Same fields as Type 4.

docs.title: Type 12: Addressed Safety Related Message
docs.text: Field Type Range Description seqno Integer 0–3 Sequence number dest_mmsi Integer 9 digits Destination MMSI retransmit Boolean – Retransmit flag text String – Safety related text

docs.title: Type 13: Safety Related Acknowledge
docs.text: Same fields as Type 7.

docs.text: Field Type Range Description text String – Safety related text

docs.title: Type 15: Interrogation
docs.text: Field Type Range Description mmsi1 Integer 9 digits Interrogated MMSI 1 type1_1 Integer 1–27 First message type requested from station 1 offset1_1 Integer – Reply slot offset for first request type1_2 Integer 1–27 Second message type requested from station 1 (if present) offset1_2 Integer – Reply slot offset for second request mmsi2 Integer 9 digits Interrogated MMSI 2 (if present) type2_1 Integer 1–27 First message type requested from station 2 offset2_1 Integer – Reply slot offset for first request

docs.text: Field Type Range Description lon Float ±180° Longitude (1/600 degree resolution); omitted when not available (181°) lat Float ±90° Latitude (1/600 degree resolution); omitted when not available (91°) data String hex DGNSS data

docs.title: Type 18: Standard Class B CS Position Report
docs.text: Field Type Range Description reserved Integer – Reserved speed Float 0–102.2 knots Speed over ground; omitted when not available (102.3) accuracy Boolean – Position accuracy lon Float ±180° Longitude; omitted when not available (181°) lat Float ±90° Latitude; omitted when not available (91°) course Float 0–359.9° Course over ground; omitted when not available (360) heading Integer 0–359° True heading; omitted when not available (511) second Integer 0–59 UTC second; omitted when not available (60) power Boolean – Transmit power flag (M.1371-6 Table 68; 0 = high, 1 = low). See note 5 for sub-fields.

docs.text:
Aligned to M.1371-6 Table 69: the 8-bit reserved and 4-bit regional fields are now spare per spec.

Field Type Range Description speed Float 0–102.2 knots Speed over ground; omitted when not available (102.3) accuracy Boolean – Position accuracy lon Float ±180° Longitude; omitted when not available (181°) lat Float ±90° Latitude; omitted when not available (91°) course Float 0–359.9° Course over ground; omitted when not available (360) heading Integer 0–359° True heading; omitted when not available (511) second Integer 0–59 UTC second; omitted when not available (60) shipname String 20 chars Vessel name shiptype Integer 0–99 Ship type code shiptype_text String See note 3 Ship type description to_bow Integer 0–511 m Dimension to bow to_stern Integer 0–511 m Dimension to stern to_port Integer 0–63 m Dimension to port to_starboard Integer 0–63 m Dimension to starboard epfd Integer 0–8 EPFD type epfd_text String See note 2 EPFD description raim Boolean – RAIM flag dte Boolean – DTE flag assigned Boolean – Assigned mode flag

docs.text: Field Type Range Description aid_type Integer 0–31 Aid type aid_type_text String See note 4 Aid type description name String 20 chars Name of aid accuracy Boolean – Position accuracy lon Float ±180° Longitude; omitted when not available (181°) lat Float ±90° Latitude; omitted when not available (91°) to_bow Integer 0–511 m Dimension to bow to_stern Integer 0–511 m Dimension to stern to_port Integer 0–63 m Dimension to port to_starboard Integer 0–63 m Dimension to starboard epfd Integer 0–8 EPFD type epfd_text String See note 2 EPFD description second Integer 0–59 UTC second; omitted when not available (60) off_position Boolean – Off position indicator aton_status Integer 0–255 AtoN status bits (M.1371-6 Table 71, 8-bit, AtoN-specific status per IALA R0126). Field Type Range Description channel_a Integer – Channel A number channel_b Integer – Channel B number txrx Integer – Tx/Rx mode power Boolean – Transmit power flag (0 = high, 1 = low) addressed Boolean – Addressed flag band_a Boolean – Channel A band (0 = default, 1 = 12.5 kHz allowed) band_b Boolean – Channel B band zonesize Integer – Size of transitional zone

If addressed = true:

Field Type Range Description dest1 Integer 9 digits Destination MMSI 1 dest2 Integer 9 digits Destination MMSI 2

Field Type Range Description ne_lon Float ±180° NE longitude ne_lat Float ±90° NE latitude sw_lon Float ±180° SW longitude sw_lat Float ±90° SW latitude

docs.text: Field Type Range Description ne_lon Float ±180° NE longitude ne_lat Float ±90° NE latitude sw_lon Float ±180° SW longitude sw_lat Float ±90° SW latitude station_type Integer – Station type shiptype Integer 0–99 Ship type code shiptype_text String See note 3 Ship type description txrx Integer – Tx/Rx mode interval Integer – Reporting interval quiet Integer minutes Quiet time

docs.title: Type 24: Static Data Report
docs.text:
Message Type 24 Part A:

Field Type Range Description partno Integer 0 Part number, always 0 for Part A shipname String 20 chars Name of the vessel

Message Type 24 Part B:

Field Type Range Description partno Integer 1 Part number, always 1 for Part B shiptype Integer 0–99 Type of ship and cargo shiptype_text String See note 3 Description of ship type vendorid String 3 chars Manufacturer's ID model Integer 0–15 Equipment model code serial Integer 0–999999 Unit serial number callsign String 7 chars Vessel radio callsign to_bow Integer 0–511 m Distance from GPS to bow to_stern Integer 0–511 m Distance from GPS to stern to_port Integer 0–63 m Distance from GPS to port to_starboard Integer 0–63 m Distance from GPS to starboard mothership_mmsi Integer 9 digits MMSI of mothership (only for auxiliary craft, MMSI prefix 98) epfd Integer 0–8 EPFD type (M.1371-6 extended Part B; only when message length ≥ 168 bits) epfd_text String See note 2 EPFD description (only when epfd is present) vdes_capabilities Integer 0–3 VDES capabilities (M.1371-6; 0 = AIS only, 1 = VDES ASM, 2 = +VDE-TER, 3 = +VDE-SAT). Only when message length ≥ 168 bits.

docs.title: Type 25, 26: Single Slot / Multi Slot Binary Message
docs.text:
The envelope is decoded; when binary_data_flag = 1 the payload follows the same (dac, fid) layout as msg 6 (addressed) or msg 8 (broadcast) and is dispatched to the same ASM decoders — see ASM payloads below.

Field Type Range Description addressed Boolean – Addressed flag (0 = broadcast, 1 = addressed to a specific MMSI) ai_available Boolean – Application Identifier available flag (1 = ASM application data follows) dest_mmsi Integer 9 digits Destination MMSI (only when addressed = true) dac Integer – Designated Area Code (only when ai_available = true) fid Integer – Functional Identifier (only when ai_available = true)

When the (dac, fid) pair is recognised the structured ASM fields are emitted in addition (see ASM payloads). For msg 26 the trailing 20-bit communication-state block (1-bit selector followed by the 19-bit SOTDMA/ITDMA state) is decoded into the standard radio sub-fields — see note 5.

docs.title: Type 27: Long-Range AIS Broadcast
docs.text: Field Type Range Description accuracy Boolean – Position accuracy (true if <10 m) raim Boolean – RAIM flag status Integer 0–15 Navigation status status_text String See note 1 Navigation status description lon Float ±180° Longitude (1/600 degree resolution); omitted when not available (181°) lat Float ±90° Latitude (1/600 degree resolution); omitted when not available (91°) speed Integer 0–62 knots Speed over ground; omitted when not available (63) course Integer 0–359° Course over ground; omitted when not available (511) gnss Boolean – Position latency (M.1371-6; 0 = reported position latency <5 s, 1 = ≥5 s, default). Was named "GNSS position status" in pre-M.1371-6 revisions; field name kept for backward compatibility.

docs.title: Type 28: AtoN Report (single-slot)
docs.text:
ITU-R M.1371-6 §A7-3.26, Table 84.

Field Type Range Description second Integer 0–59 UTC second; omitted when not available (60) lon Float ±180° Longitude (1/600000° resolution); omitted when not available (181°) lat Float ±90° Latitude (1/600000° resolution); omitted when not available (91°) restricted_use Integer 0–3 Restricted use flag (0 = default; 1..3 reserved for restricted use) aton_station_type Integer 0–7 AtoN station type (3-bit; lookup) virtual_aid Boolean – Virtual AtoN flag — true when aton_station_type == 4 aid_type Integer 0–31 Type of Aid to Navigation aid_type_text String See note 4 Aid type description iala_mrn Integer 0–131071 IALA AtoN Maritime Resource Name (17-bit identifier) dim_type Integer 0–15 AtoN Dimensions Type — defines what to_bow/to_stern represent (Table 84) to_bow Integer 0–511 m Dimension to bow (interpretation depends on dim_type) to_stern Integer 0–2047 m Dimension to stern (interpretation depends on dim_type) additional_flag Boolean – Additional information flag charted_status Boolean – Charted status (0 = not charted, 1 = charted) on_station_status Integer 0–15 On-station status (4-bit; lookup) aton_status Integer 0–255 AtoN status bits (8-bit, AtoN-specific status per IALA R0126) auth_flag Boolean – Authentication flag (1 = transmission authenticated)

docs.title: ASM payloads (Type 6 / Type 8)
docs.text:
For Type 6 and Type 8 messages, AIS-catcher decodes selected Application-Specific Messages (ASMs) identified by the (dac, fid) pair. When a decoder matches, the structured fields below are emitted in addition to the per-type fields (dac, fid, etc.); when no decoder matches, the raw payload is emitted as data (hex string).

Jump to: IMO/ITU-R (DAC=1) · IALA Zeni Lite Buoy (DAC=0) · Flag-state text (DAC=210/248/353) · Inland AIS (DAC=200) · IALA AtoN monitoring (DAC=235/250/366) · Sweden STM (DAC=265) · St Lawrence Seaway (DAC=316/366) · US Environmental (DAC=367)

docs.title: FID = 0: Text using 6-bit ASCII (msg 6 and 8)
docs.text: Field Type Description ack_required Boolean Acknowledgement required text_sequence Integer Sequence number for multi-part text text String Text payload

docs.title: FID = 2: Interrogation for a specified FMS (msg 6)
docs.text: Field Type Description requested_dac Integer Designated Area Code requested requested_fid Integer Functional Identifier requested

docs.title: FID = 3: Extended interrogation (msg 6)
docs.text: Field Type Description requested_dac Integer Designated Area Code requested

docs.title: FID = 4: Capability reply (msg 6)
docs.text: Field Type Description ai_available String 128-bit AI-available bitstring (ASCII '0'/'1')

docs.title: FID = 11: Legacy meteorological/hydrological (msg 8, IMO SN/Circ.236)
docs.text: Same fields as FID = 31 below (legacy encoding; superseded by FID = 31).

docs.title: FID = 16: Persons on board (msg 6, also FID 40) / VTS targets (msg 8)
docs.text:
The same (DAC=1, FID=16) slot is reused for two different payloads depending on message type.

In msg 6 (number of persons on board, also FID = 40):

Field Type Description persons Integer Number of persons on board

In msg 8 (VTS targets, IMO Circ.289 §6):

Field Type Unit Description vts_target_id_type Integer – Target ID type vts_target_id Integer or String – Target identifier (string when id_type = 2; numeric otherwise) vts_target_lat Float degrees Target latitude vts_target_lon Float degrees Target longitude vts_target_cog Integer degrees Target course over ground vts_target_timestamp Integer seconds UTC second of report vts_target_sog Integer knots Target speed over ground

docs.title: FID = 17: VTS-generated/synthetic targets (msg 8, IMO Circ.289 §6 Table 6.1/6.2)
docs.text:
Up to four synthetic targets (120 bits each) are decoded and packed into a single string.

Field Type Description targets String id,lat,lon,cog,sog;… per target. id is 7-char ASCII; lat/lon in degrees; cog in degrees; sog in tenths of a knot.

docs.text:
Both FIDs share the same layout: a header followed by up to ten sub-areas of 87 bits. Circle, rectangle and sector sub-areas are decoded into area_shapes, text sub-areas are joined into area_notice_name, polyline and polygon sub-areas are skipped.

Field Type Unit Description linkage_id Integer – Message linkage ID; omitted when 0 area_notice_type Integer – Area notice type (0–127, IMO Circ.289 Table 5.2) month Integer 1–12 Start month (UTC); omitted when not available (0) day Integer 1–31 Start day; omitted when not available (0) hour Integer 0–23 Start hour; omitted when not available (24) minute Integer 0–59 Start minute; omitted when not available (60) area_notice_duration Integer minutes Duration; omitted when not available (262143) area_notice_lat Float degrees Latitude of the first decoded shape area_notice_lon Float degrees Longitude of the first decoded shape area_shapes String – Sub-areas separated by ;. docs.text:

docs.title: Flag-state text telegrams (DAC = 210 / 248 / 353)
docs.text:
Several national / flag-state ASMs reuse the IMO Circ.236 6-bit ASCII text payload (the same encoding as DAC = 1, FID = 0). The following allocations are decoded with the same fields:

  • DAC = 210 (Cyprus), FID = 0 — text telegram
  • DAC = 248 (Malta), FID = 0 — text telegram
  • DAC = 353 (Liberia), FID = 0 — text telegram
Field Type Description linkage_id Integer Message linkage ID text String Free-text payload (6-bit ASCII)

docs.title: Sweden STM — Sea Traffic Management route (DAC = 265)
FID = 1: STM route message (msg 8)
docs.text:
Broadcast on msg 8, up to 3 slots. The route is reconstructed from a delta-encoded chain of legs (first waypoint, 0–6 delta legs, then an absolute final leg). Header-only / cancellation messages produce no fields.

Field Type Unit Description waypoints String – Reconstructed waypoints as lat,lon[;lat,lon]… planned_speed Float knots Planned speed for the final leg steering_mode Integer – Steering mode (0 = manual, 1 = heading, 2 = track)

Spec reference: https://www.e-navigation.nl/content/route-message-0

docs.title: FID = 1: Meteorological/hydrological (msg 6 and 8)
docs.text:
message_id selects the sub-payload (1 = weather, 2 = wind, 3 = water level, 6 = water flow). All variants share a common header.

Common header (all variants):

Field Type Unit Description message_id Integer – Sub-message identifier month Integer – UTC month day Integer – UTC day hour Integer – UTC hour minute Integer – UTC minute station_id String – Station identifier (7-char ASCII) lon Float degrees Longitude lat Float degrees Latitude

message_id = 1 (weather) adds:

Field Type Unit Description wspeed Float knots Wind speed (0.1 kn); omitted above 101.3 kn (1014 and 1023 are not-available codes) wgust Float knots Wind gust (0.1 kn); omitted above 101.3 kn (1014 and 1023 are not-available codes) wdir Integer degrees Wind direction; omitted when not available (511) barometric_pressure Float hPa Barometric pressure (0.1 hPa); omitted when not available (16383) air_temperature Float °C Air temperature; omitted when not available dew_point Float °C Dew point; omitted when not available visibility_km Float km Horizontal visibility; omitted when not available (255) watertemp Float °C Water temperature; omitted when not available

Field Type Unit Description water_level_type Integer – Water level type waterlevel Float metres Water level reference_datum Integer – Reference datum reading_type Integer – Reading type

message_id = 6 (water flow) adds:

Field Type Unit Description water_flow Integer – Water flow

docs.title: FID = 2: Lock scheduling (msg 8)
docs.text:
Field Type Unit Description message_id Integer – Sub-message: 1 = lock schedule, 2 = vessel lock ETA. Other values expose only message_id.

message_id = 1 (lock schedule) adds:

Field Type Unit Description month Integer 1–12 Schedule month (UTC); omitted when not available (0) day Integer 1–31 Schedule day; omitted when not available (0) hour Integer 0–23 Schedule hour; omitted when not available (24) minute Integer 0–59 Schedule minute; omitted when not available (60) lock_id String – Lock name (7 chars); omitted when empty lon Float degrees Lock longitude (1/60000°); omitted when not available lat Float degrees Lock latitude (1/60000°); omitted when not available lock_schedule String – Up to six entries separated by ;, each name,direction,MM-DDTHH:MMZ with the direction bit as sent (0 or 1). Entries with an empty name are skipped.

message_id = 2 (vessel lock ETA) adds the same month, day, hour and minute and:

Field Type Unit Description vessel_name String – Vessel name (15 chars) last_location String – Last reported location (7 chars) last_ata String UTC Actual time of arrival there (MM-DDTHH:MMZ); omitted when the month is 0 first_lock String – Next lock (7 chars) first_lock_eta String UTC ETA at the next lock; omitted when the month is 0 second_lock String – Lock after that (7 chars) second_lock_eta String UTC ETA at the second lock; omitted when the month is 0 delay_lock String – Lock where a delay is expected (7 chars)

Seaway text fields pack several tokens into one field with @ separators; @ is read as a space, so B@ N@ D@ becomes B N D. Empty strings are omitted.

docs.title: Configuration Keys
docs.text: The keys the managed hub edits, generated from its editor schema. They live in the config.json that -C reads and managed mode (-E) keeps; JSON Configuration shows the structure with examples, and the command line accepts more than is listed here: see the settings page linked from each section. "Only with" marks a key that applies for one choice of another key in the same object.

docs.title: Main section
docs.text: Key Type Default Values Description config string – "aiscatcher" Identifies the file; required version number – 1 Format version; required receiver object[] – One object per receiver, see Receiver udp object[] – UDP outputs, see UDP http object[] – HTTP outputs, see HTTP mqtt object[] – MQTT outputs, see MQTT tcp object[] – TCP Client outputs, see TCP Client tcp_listener object[] – TCP Server outputs, see TCP Server db object[] – Database outputs, see Database server object[] – Viewer outputs, see Viewer engine string "off" on · off Managed mode: whether the receivers run; the Start and Stop buttons write it control object – Managed mode, see Managed mode sharing boolean false Share messages with the community map sharing_key string – Leave empty to share anonymously sharing_zone string[] [] No zones — receives from all inputs timeout false or number false (60 when set) 1 – 3600 Stop the receiver after this many seconds timeout_only_when_idle boolean false Watchdog: counts only while input is idle screen string "0" 0 Off · 1 NMEA · 2 NMEA + details · 3 JSON with NMEA · 4 JSON (compact) · 5 JSON (full) Messages written to standard output: the journal under systemd, the container log under Docker verbose_time number 3 1 – 3600 How often a receiver with Verbose on logs its message counts; one interval for all receivers

docs.title: Receiver
docs.text:
Each entry of receiver is one object. input selects the device and the device section of the same name inside the object configures it.

Only with input = RTLSDR or AIRSPY or AIRSPYHF or HACKRF or HYDRASDR nmea_channel string – AB Channel letters in the NMEA output; AB for software that only knows A and B. Only with channel = CD serial string – Pick a device by serial number. Only with input = RTLSDR or AIRSPY or AIRSPYHF or HYDRASDR or HACKRF active boolean true Active verbose boolean false Log message counts at the interval set under Output › Screen zone string[] [] Routes this receiver to outputs sharing a zone

docs.text:

docs.title: Managed mode
docs.text: Managed mode (-E) reads the same file. The server beside the control panel, on the panel's port plus one, is the entry of services marked "main": true: it takes a server's keys (api, mcp, system, geojson, kml, metrics, keys, public, view) and the Viewer options (realtime, replay, msg, decoder, log, station, station_link, webcontrol_http, mbtiles, …), never a port; the map is always on it. It loads no plugins and no about page, which go on another server, and has no log: the panel shows it. How ships are kept is tracking (file, backup, history, track_time, track_memory, expire, max_ships, cutoff, places), and the default station is station 0 of stations. control.wizard (boolean) shows the setup wizard on the next visit; the hub stores its password under control itself; leave those keys alone. control.tls (cert, key) puts the panel itself on HTTPS. A file from before, with the viewer under control.viewer, is read as it is and brought to this layout by the panel when it saves.

docs.title: Python — aiscat
docs.text:
aiscat is a Python package that exposes the AIS-catcher decoder as a library. Output dictionaries match the AIS-catcher JSON format field-for-field, so anything you've built around the documented JSON output works the same when the source becomes a Python iterator.

It is built for fast, complete decoding of AIS NMEA from Python: all standard message types (1–28), multi-part AIVDM reassembly, country-code resolution from MMSI prefix, lookup-table text fields populated from the same tables AIS-catcher uses, and decoding of binary application messages (type 6 and 8 ASMs across IMO, IALA, USA, and inland-waterway DAC/FID payloads).

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install aiscat

Pre-built wheels are published on PyPI for Linux (x86_64, aarch64, armv7l), macOS (Apple Silicon), and Windows (x86_64, ARM64), Python 3.9–3.14.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
One-shot decoding:

import aiscat

aiscat.decode("!AIVDM,1,1,,A,15MgK45P3@G?fl0E`JbR0OwT0@MS,0*4E")
# {'type': 1, 'mmsi': 366730000, 'channel': 'A', 'rxuxtime': 1777739134.027,
#  'lat': 37.803802, 'lon': -122.392532, 'speed': 20.8, 'course': 51.3,
#  'status': 5, 'status_text': 'Moored', ...}

Streaming from a file, stdin, TCP, or UDP source — the helpers wire up the I/O loop and yield decoded messages:

for msg in aiscat.from_file("session.nmea"):
    print(msg["mmsi"], msg["lat"], msg["lon"])

for msg in aiscat.from_tcp("ais.example.com", 4001):
    handle(msg)

For full control, use Decoder directly: feed(bytes) parses NMEA / JSON / binary input out of the buffer, and next() pops one decoded message.

docs.title: Timestamps
docs.text:
Each decoded message carries two timestamps:

  • rxuxtime — the time aiscat decoded the message (i.e. now). Always present.
  • toa — the time (if any) carried in the input. For JSON input that's the toa or rxuxtime field (toa wins if both are present); for NMEA it's the tag-block c: field. Omitted from the output if the input had none.

This split makes it unambiguous which clock you are looking at when chaining decoders or replaying recordings — the local decode time and any preserved upstream time are kept in separate fields rather than overwriting each other.

docs.title: Output formats
docs.text:
The format= kwarg selects what next() (and the helpers) return. Dict-shaped formats are convenient for in-Python consumption; bytes-shaped formats skip the dict allocation and are several times faster — useful when forwarding the data to a file, socket, database, or another AIS-catcher instance.

Format Returns Equivalent to Notes "dictionary" (default) dict AIS-catcher -o 5 (parsed) Full decoded fields. "annotated" dict AIS-catcher -o 6 (parsed) Each scalar wrapped as {value, unit, description, text}. "json" bytes AIS-catcher -o 5 Full decoded JSON, ready to write/send. "json_nmea" bytes AIS-catcher -o 3 Slim JSON envelope wrapping the original NMEA — the relay/passthrough format. "nmea" bytes AIS-catcher -n / -o 1 The raw AIVDM/AIVDO line(s). "nmea_tag" bytes — NMEA prefixed with an IEC 61162-450 tag block carrying source + timestamp. "binary" bytes — AIS-catcher's native 0xac binary packet format (compact, suitable for inter-process transport).

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: For live decode of a single station (~50 msg/s) any AIS library is fast enough. aiscat earns its keep when throughput matters: historical replay, multi-receiver aggregation, batch analysis, and research workloads on millions to billions of messages. On a single Apple M-series core it reaches ≈1.76 M msg/s for dictionary output and ≈5.5 M msg/s for nmea/binary, tracking the native AIS-catcher CLI closely.

docs.title: More
docs.text:
• Source, examples (CSV, MQTT, Kafka, TCP relay), benchmarks, and the full API reference: github.com/jvde-github/AIS-catcher/tree/main/python
  • Licence is GPLv3, inherited from AIS-catcher.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text: Out of the box, AIS-catcher shows the ships it hears on a map. It can do much more: feed other applications, and serve as the base you build your own on. A second receiver joining the same installation, a notification on your phone when a ship comes in, a script that logs every arrival, an assistant that answers questions about the harbour. All of it is built in.

docs.title: Connecting your station to other tools
docs.text:
Multiple receivers as stations, geofencing with places, queries over the API and from an AI assistant, and home automation with Home Assistant and webhooks. One example runs through every part: a station at Harwich, where the Stour and the Orwell meet the North Sea.

Part 1, 6 minutes Running multiple receivers at one or more stations Run more than one receiver from one AIS-catcher. Receivers in one place are one station, receivers elsewhere are stations of their own, each with its range and figures, and the ships they hear together form one picture.

Part 2, 6 minutes Geofencing: monitoring ports and guard zones Places are the geofences of AIS-catcher: a port, a guard zone across the harbour mouth, any area you draw on the map. Your station then keeps track of who is inside, who came and went and who is on the way, and announces each crossing.

Part 3, 8 minutes Querying your station with the API and MCP Every station answers questions: over HTTP for your scripts and spreadsheets, and in plain words through an AI assistant. The same data, the same places, two ways to ask.

Part 4, 7 minutes Home automation with Home Assistant and webhooks Turn the events of your station into automations: a notification when a ship crosses the harbour mouth, a light when your ferry is in, the ships in port on a dashboard. With Home Assistant over MQTT, or anything that takes a webhook.

docs.title: 3. The API and MCP
docs.text: Part 1 Multiple receivers Part 2 Geofencing Part 3 API and MCP Part 4 Home automation

docs.title: Querying your station with the API and MCP
docs.text:
Every station answers questions: over HTTP for your scripts and spreadsheets, and in plain words through an AI assistant. The same data, the same places, two ways to ask.

Connecting your station to other tools, part 3 · 8 minutes to read

The first of four questions to the station at Harwich: the assistant calls two tools, and the answer comes from the station's own data.

Four questions to the station at Harwich. Each one is answered by a tool; the third column is the same question over HTTP, and the last the answer. The answers come from the station's own data.

Question Tool the assistant calls API request The answer Which ships are waiting at anchor? find_places {"type": "anchorage"}get_place {"uuid": "3edb107e…"} GET /api/v1/places?type=anchorage NORDIC TRADER, a Norwegian tanker, has been at anchor in Haven anchorage since 12:51. It reports Felixstowe as its destination. Who came through the harbour mouth in the last hour? place_visits {"uuid": "508906af…", "hours": 1} GET /api/v1/places/508906af…/visits?hours=1 Three ships: MAAS CARRIER came in at 12:54, HOOK EXPRESS went out at 13:02, and the pilot boat STOUR PILOT crossed three times. Where did MAAS CARRIER go? vessel_visits {"mmsi": 244870001}vessel_track {"mmsi": 244870001} GET /api/v1/vessels/244870001/track It came in through the harbour mouth at 12:54, entered Felixstowe at 12:58 and has been moored at Trinity Terminal since 13:02. Is my station healthy? health {}list_receivers {} GET /api/v1/health Yes. The engine and its receiver pass their checks, and the Harwich station was heard a second ago.

Your station knows a lot: which ships it hears, where they went, who called at which port, what happened and when. There are two ways to ask. Programs ask over HTTP, through the API. People ask in plain words, through an AI assistant connected over MCP, the Model Context Protocol. Both read the same data, including the stations and places of the earlier parts of this series.

docs.title: Switch them on
docs.text:
In the dashboard open Settings, then Services and Main, the server beside the dashboard. Switch on API and MCP, and System as well if questions about the station itself, its receivers, health and log, should be answered too. On a standard installation Main can be reached from your network, so Access asks who may read it: Open for anyone on the network, or Keys for those you give one with New key. System needs Keys. Then Save changes.

Services, Main: each service is a switch. The screenshots come from a test installation on its own ports.

On a standard installation the dashboard is on port 8118 and the Main server, with the map, the API and MCP, on 8119. Without the dashboard the switches follow the server's port, and the server stays on this machine until you give it keys or make it public:

Command line

AIS-catcher -d 00000001 -N 8100 api on mcp on system on

config.json

"services": [ { "port": 8100, "api": true, "mcp": true, "system": true } ]

docs.title: In plain words: MCP
docs.text:
MCP is an open standard for handing an assistant a set of tools. Your station offers up to twenty-two: find vessels, look up a place, list its visits, read the events, check the receivers. The assistant picks the tools, reads the answers and writes its reply. Every tool only reads; none can change a setting, stop anything or send anything out.

For Claude Code on the station itself, one line connects it. Try the API, under Connect an assistant in its MCP view, shows the same line with your station's address, and with the key when Main uses Keys:

Terminal

claude mcp add --transport http aiscatcher http://127.0.0.1:8119/mcp

Other assistants that speak MCP over HTTP take the same address. Here is a real exchange with the test station, asked in Claude Code:

Which ships are waiting at anchor off Harwich, and which ships are bound for Felixstowe? Keep the answer short.

Claude called six tools:

  1. find_places {"q": "Harwich"}
  2. find_places {"type": "anchorage"}
  3. find_places {"q": "Felixstowe"}
  4. get_place {"uuid": "3edb107e-96d4-4da8-9865-fac336fcf2c4"}
  5. vessels_in_area {"bbox": "0.5,51.3,2.5,52.5", "limit": 25}
  6. get_place {"uuid": "cfabeebc-3490-4863-aeea-f61984ed42a0"}

and answered:

At anchor off Harwich (Haven anchorage): NORDIC TRADER, a Norwegian tanker (IMO 9765433), at anchor with 8.5 m draught.

Bound for Felixstowe: NORDIC TRADER, whose destination is "FELIXSTOWE". It is the ship waiting at anchor. MAAS CARRIER, a Dutch cargo ship (IMO 9876543), with destination "GB FXT" (Felixstowe's port code). It is already moored inside the port.

ORWELL FISHER is fishing inside the anchorage area and HOOK EXPRESS is passing at 20 kn. Neither is anchored, and neither is going to Felixstowe.

— Claude Code, connected to the test station over MCP

Right on every count, including the two ships it left out and why. The places did the hard part: an anchorage and a port are named areas the assistant can look up, not coordinates it has to guess.

Tools What they answer search_vessels Vessels by name, call sign, MMSI or IMO number vessels_in_area vessels_near Vessels in a box, or near a point list_vessels Vessels by any of the API's filters together: destination, speed, distance, station get_vessel vessel_track vessel_visits One vessel in full, where it went, where it called find_places get_place place_visits Ports and other places, and who came and went list_stations station_statistics data_status The stations and their figures, and how fresh the data is recent_events Safety messages, new destinations and statuses, arrivals and departures list_aircraft get_aircraft Aircraft, when an ADS-B receiver feeds the station system_status health list_receivers list_outputs read_log system_events The installation itself, with System switched on

docs.title: Over HTTP: the API
docs.text:
Every tool above is one request of the API, under /api/v1. The quickest way to look around is Try the API, under Services: pick an endpoint, fill in what it asks and press Send. Below the answer is the curl line that does the same from a terminal.

Try the API, looking up the port of Felixstowe by name.

A few of the questions programs ask most, here of an Open Main; with Keys, add -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY":

Terminal

# the ships within two nautical miles of the harbour mouth
curl "http://raspberrypi.local:8119/api/v1/vessels?near=51.94,1.30&radius_nm=2"

# a port by name, for its uuid
curl "http://raspberrypi.local:8119/api/v1/places?q=Felixstowe"

# who came through the harbour mouth, with times and whether they stopped
curl "http://raspberrypi.local:8119/api/v1/places/508906af-27ba-4219-9f92-6fee2b610516/visits"

# where a ship went, as GeoJSON for QGIS or geojson.io
curl "http://raspberrypi.local:8119/api/v1/vessels/244870001/track?format=geojson"

Answer to the visits request, the newest row

{
  "mmsi": 235870003,
  "name": "STOUR PILOT",
  "entered": "2026-10-23T12:21:43Z",
  "left": "2026-10-23T12:22:48Z",
  "inside": false,
  "call": true,
  ...
}

Every list has its rows under data, and under meta how many there are and, where there is more, next: the request for the following page. Times are UTC, distances nautical miles and speeds knots. A problem comes back as application/problem+json with a detail that says what to fix, and /api/v1/openapi.json describes every endpoint for Postman, Insomnia or a client generator.

docs.title: Following what happens
docs.text:
/api/v1/events is the station's journal: arrivals, departures, safety messages, new destinations. A script that keeps asking for meta.poll sees every event once, and a 410 tells it the journal started again. This one prints the ships crossing the harbour mouth, with nothing but Python's standard library:

follow.py

import json, time, urllib.error, urllib.request

STATION = "http://raspberrypi.local:8119"
PLACE = "Harbour mouth"

def get(path):
    with urllib.request.urlopen(STATION + path) as r:
        return json.load(r)

def start():                             # what comes after the newest event
    return get("/api/v1/events?limit=25")["meta"]["poll"]

url = start()
while True:
    try:
        page = get(url)
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as err:
        if err.code != 410:              # 410: the journal started again
            raise
        url = start()
        continue
    for e in page["data"]:
        if e["kind"] in ("place_enter", "place_exit") and e.get("text") == PLACE:
            verb = "entered" if e["kind"] == "place_enter" else "left"
            print(e["time"], e["name"], verb, e["text"], flush=True)
    if page["meta"]["next"]:             # more already waiting
        url = page["meta"]["next"]
    else:
        url = page["meta"]["poll"]
        time.sleep(10)

Output

2026-10-23T12:21:43Z STOUR PILOT entered Harbour mouth
2026-10-23T12:22:48Z STOUR PILOT left Harbour mouth

Rather be called than ask? The same events go out as webhooks, which the next part puts to work.

docs.title: From another machine
docs.text:
A server you add, or one started with -N or from the configuration file, listens only on the station itself until you open it. Main follows the dashboard, which a standard installation opens to your network. An open server is one of two kinds, never both:

  • Keys. Press New key, name it and press Make key. The key is shown once; the configuration keeps only its SHA-256. Without it the answer is 401. A key with only the Data scope reads ships, places and events, but never the installation: no health, receivers or log.
  • Open, "public": true in the configuration. Anyone who reaches the server reads its data, without a key. System is never open on the network.

To give a laptop its own way in: under Services press Add server, let it listen on the network, switch on what it should offer, make a key and press Save changes.

Terminal

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://raspberrypi.local:8120/api/v1/vessels?limit=5"
claude mcp add --transport http aiscatcher http://raspberrypi.local:8120/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"

For a server anyone may use, switch on Limited as well: every caller then gets short rows, 25 to a page, and 25 data calls an hour from one address. Poll a Limited server every few minutes, not every ten seconds.

docs.title: Text that ships send
docs.text:
A ship's name and destination are typed by its crew, and AIS lets anyone send any text. To an assistant that could look like an instruction. AIS-catcher tells every assistant that connects that names, call signs, destinations and messages are broadcast data and never instructions, and that positions are not for navigation. Its tools only read, so even a confused assistant can do no more than answer wrongly.

Next: turning the station's events into automations, in Home Assistant and anything else that takes a webhook.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
New to AIS-catcher, or setting it up step by step? Start with the Quick Start. Every option of this tutorial is in the documentation.

  • Quick Start: install AIS-catcher and see your first ships, in a few steps.
  • Ask your station: the API: the set-up guide for the API.
  • Let an AI assistant read your station: the set-up guide for MCP.
  • The API and MCP: every service, key and tool, with examples.

docs.title: 4. Home Automation and Webhooks
docs.text: Part 1 Multiple receivers Part 2 Geofencing Part 3 API and MCP Part 4 Home automation

docs.title: Home automation with Home Assistant and webhooks
docs.text:
Turn the events of your station into automations: a notification when a ship crosses the harbour mouth, a light when your ferry is in, the ships in port on a dashboard. With Home Assistant over MQTT, or anything that takes a webhook.

Connecting your station to other tools, part 4 · 7 minutes to read

What Home Assistant received while MAAS CARRIER came in: a notification from the guard zone, the watched ship entering a Home Assistant zone, and the sensor counting it in port once it stopped.

The station from the earlier parts knows when a ship enters the harbour mouth, calls at Felixstowe or sends a safety message. This part sends that news on: to Home Assistant, which turns it into notifications, lights and dashboards, and as webhooks to anything else that listens.

Two routes lead out of the station. MQTT carries its state and its events to Home Assistant, which finds everything by itself. Webhooks post each event to an address you choose, for Home Assistant or any other tool.

AIS-catcher place_enter, place_exit safety, status, destination and its state: vessels, stations, receivers MQTT Your MQTT broker state kept, events passed on discovery Home Assistant sensors, Events, vessel trackers webhooks: one signed POST per event Your automation Home Assistant, Node-RED, n8n The broker keeps the station's state for Home Assistant to read whenever it starts; a webhook is one POST per event, signed when you give it a secret.

docs.title: Home Assistant over MQTT
docs.text:
MQTT is the message broker most Home Assistant installations already run for their sensors. In the dashboard:

  1. Open Settings, then Services and Home Assistant.
  2. Enter the Broker, for instance mqtt://homeassistant.local:1883, with the User and Password it asks for.
  3. Leave Home Assistant discovery on. Under Watched vessels, put the MMSI of each ship you want to follow, one per line.
  4. Press Save changes.

Services, Home Assistant: a broker, and the vessels to follow.

config.json

"mqtt_state": {
    "url": "mqtt://homeassistant.local:1883",
    "username": "ais",
    "password": "secret",
    "watch": [244870001]
}

Command line

AIS-catcher -d 00000001 -W mqtt://homeassistant.local:1883 USERNAME ais PASSWORD secret WATCH 244870001

With discovery on there is nothing to set up in Home Assistant. Under Settings, Devices & services, MQTT a device called AIS-catcher appears, with:

  • Vessels and Message rate: how busy the station is.
  • Receiving, and for each receiver whether it is streaming: the station's health.
  • For each station, whether it is online and how many vessels it heard in the last hour.
  • Events: every arrival, departure, safety message and change of destination, as it happens.
  • A device tracker for each watched vessel, with its position, speed and when it was last heard.

The device in Home Assistant. The watched container ship reads "Felixstowe": it is inside a Home Assistant zone of that name.

Note

The station's position is never published to the broker. A station that is private on the community map stays private here too.

docs.title: A notification when a ship comes through the harbour mouth
docs.text:
The Events entity changes with every event. Its attributes say what happened: event_type is place_enter or place_exit for a place, text is the place's name, name and mmsi are the ship's.

automations.yaml

- alias: Ship in the harbour mouth
  triggers:
    - trigger: state
      entity_id: event.ais_catcher_events
      not_from: unavailable
  conditions:
    - condition: template
      value_template: >
        {{ trigger.to_state.attributes.event_type == 'place_enter'
           and trigger.to_state.attributes.text == 'Harbour mouth' }}
  actions:
    - action: notify.mobile_app_your_phone
      data:
        title: Harbour mouth
        message: "{{ trigger.to_state.attributes.name }} is in the harbour mouth"

Use your own notifier in place of notify.mobile_app_your_phone. not_from: unavailable keeps the automation quiet while Home Assistant starts. If you rename places now and then, compare trigger.to_state.attributes.place instead: the place's id, which never changes.

One notification for each crossing, about ten seconds after it: AIS-catcher waits for the next position to confirm it.

docs.title: When your ferry is in
docs.text:
A watched vessel is a device tracker, so Home Assistant's own zones work on it. Draw a zone around the port in Settings, Areas, labels & zones and the tracker's state becomes the zone's name once the ship is inside:

automations.yaml

- alias: MAAS CARRIER in Felixstowe
  triggers:
    - trigger: zone
      entity_id: device_tracker.ais_catcher_vessel_244870001
      zone: zone.felixstowe
      event: enter
  actions:
    - action: light.turn_on
      target:
        entity_id: light.hallway

Look up the tracker's entity id on the device page: it carries the ship's MMSI or its name, depending on what the station had heard when Home Assistant first saw it. A zone is a circle and works only for watched ships. A place has the port's real outline, knows whether the ship has stopped, and works for every ship.

docs.title: The ships in port, on a dashboard
docs.text:
For counts, ask the station directly. With the API switched on, every place answers with the number of ships inside it:

configuration.yaml

rest:
  - resource: http://raspberrypi.local:8119/api/v1/places/cfabeebc-3490-4863-aeea-f61984ed42a0
    scan_interval: 60
    sensor:
      - name: Ships in Felixstowe
        value_template: "{{ value_json.vessels_inside }}"
        unit_of_measurement: ships

A ship counts as inside a port once it has stopped there, so ships steaming through do not push the number up. A server that uses keys needs one from every caller: add headers: {Authorization: "Bearer ..."}. An Open server needs none.

docs.title: Webhooks, for everything else
docs.text:
A webhook posts each event to an address as it happens. Home Assistant takes them, and so do Node-RED, n8n and most automation tools. Add one under Services, Webhooks, or in the configuration:

config.json

"webhooks": [
    { "url": "http://homeassistant.local:8123/api/webhook/ais-events",
      "events": ["place_enter", "place_exit"] },
    { "url": "https://example.org/hooks/ais", "events": ["safety", "system"], "secret": "whsec_..." }
]

The body is the event itself:

POST body

{ "id": "evt_1792744453_3", "time": "2026-10-23T11:54:13Z", "kind": "place_enter", "level": "notice",
  "mmsi": 244870001, "name": "MAAS CARRIER", "place": "508906af-27ba-4219-9f92-6fee2b610516",
  "text": "Harbour mouth", "lat": 51.935364, "lon": 1.315287 }

In Home Assistant a webhook trigger picks it up, no MQTT needed:

automations.yaml

- alias: Ship left the harbour mouth
  triggers:
    - trigger: webhook
      webhook_id: ais-events
      allowed_methods: [POST]
      local_only: true
  conditions:
    - condition: template
      value_template: "{{ trigger.json.kind == 'place_exit' and trigger.json.text == 'Harbour mouth' }}"
  actions:
    - action: notify.mobile_app_your_phone
      data:
        message: "{{ trigger.json.name }} left the harbour mouth"
  • Signed. With a secret, each request carries a signature as Standard Webhooks describes it, which their libraries check in one call.
  • Once per event. A beacon that repeats its safety text every minute is posted once, and again only after half an hour.
  • Retried. An address that does not answer is tried again, from five seconds up to an hour apart, while the other webhooks carry on.
  • At once. A saved webhook starts posting without restarting AIS-catcher.

From antenna to automation: stations for every antenna, geofences for the water, the API and MCP to ask about it, and automations to act on it. If you build something with your station, tell us in the forum.

docs.title: 2. Geofencing with Places
docs.text: Part 1 Multiple receivers Part 2 Geofencing Part 3 API and MCP Part 4 Home automation

docs.title: Geofencing: monitoring ports and guard zones
docs.text:
Places are the geofences of AIS-catcher: a port, a guard zone across the harbour mouth, any area you draw on the map. Your station then keeps track of who is inside, who came and went and who is on the way, and announces each crossing.

Connecting your station to other tools, part 2 · 6 minutes to read

The example: a port with its terminal, a guard zone across the harbour mouth and an anchorage offshore, drawn around the station at Harwich, the green dot; the dark line is the way the container ship MAAS CARRIER came in, by the clock in Harwich.

To an AIS receiver a ship is a dot with a name. You see it move, and that is about it. Geofencing changes that. Draw a few areas on the map, which AIS-catcher calls places, and the dots start telling stories: this ship came in through the harbour mouth, that one is waiting at anchor, a third is on its way to the port you care about.

Note

The ships in this series are a scripted replay in a test installation. Their names and numbers are made up, the behaviour of AIS-catcher is not.

docs.title: A port and a guard zone
docs.text:
Two kinds of geofence do most of the work, and they behave differently on purpose.

  • A port, like Felixstowe, with its UN/LOCODE GBFXT. A ship that steams through without stopping has not called there. Only a ship that stops counts, and ships that report the port as their destination are listed as expected.
  • A guard zone, like the harbour mouth: any area you want to be told about. Every ship that crosses it counts, stopped or not, and each crossing is announced.

A port can have parts: Trinity Terminal is drawn as part of Felixstowe, so a ship alongside is at the terminal and in the port at the same time. There are more types: berths, anchorages, marinas, moorings, traffic sectors and whole waters such as a strait. The places documentation lists them all.

Type A visit counts In the ticker Port After the ship has stopped for a minute Arrivals and departures, as routine Terminal, berth After a stop Not announced: the port already is Anchorage After a stop Not announced Guard zone Every passage Entering and leaving, as a notice ⚠

docs.title: Drawing one
docs.text:
1. Open the dashboard, then Settings and Places. Places are on from the start, kept in a places folder beside the configuration; an older installation asks to switch them on when you add the first one.
  2. Press New place, give it a name and a type, and draw its outline on the map.
  3. Save. The place is live at once, on the map and for every ship already inside it.
The Places editor. The guard zone is a plain rectangle across the entrance: a few straight edges are all a place needs.

Each place is a small GeoJSON file, so outlines can come from elsewhere too: Import…, in the menu beside New place, takes a Feature from any GIS tool or from OpenStreetMap, and Paste shape, while you edit a place, replaces just its outline. Without the dashboard, point AIS-catcher at a folder of place files:

Command line

AIS-catcher -d 00000001 -N 8100 PLACES /home/pi/places

config.json

"tracking": { "places": "/home/pi/places" },
"services": [ { "port": 8100 } ]

docs.title: One arrival, as the station saw it
docs.text:
The container ship MAAS CARRIER comes in from the North Sea, bound for "GB FXT". This is what the station recorded, by the clock in Harwich:

  • 12:52 First heard south of the harbour mouth at 10 knots. Its destination already matches Felixstowe, so the port lists it under Expected.
  • 12:54 Enters the Harbour mouth. A guard zone, so the ticker shows a notice.
  • 12:56 Leaves the harbour mouth, two minutes and ten seconds later.
  • 12:58 Enters Felixstowe, announced as routine.
  • 13:00 Inside Trinity Terminal. The ship's card now names the terminal as its location.
  • 13:02 Reports itself moored.
  • 13:03 Stopped for a minute: the stay becomes a call, and the ship counts as inside the port.

Past events in the web viewer. Notices from the guard zone carry the ⚠ mark. The pilot boat crossed it twice while the container ship came in.

Click a ship and its card says where it is now, in words rather than coordinates. When a ship lies inside several places at once, the most specific is named first: the terminal before the port.

The ship's card: at Trinity Terminal, bound for Felixstowe, which it reported as GB FXT.

Click a place and you get its ships, in tabs: who is Inside, who Left, who Arrived lately, the Visits with their times, the ships Nearby, and for a port the ships Expected. Point at a place's marker to see its outline.

Felixstowe, with the container ship inside once it has stopped. Pointing at the marker draws the outline.

docs.title: Who is on the way
docs.text:
Crews type their destination by hand, and they type it in many ways. AIS-catcher matches it to your ports, first by UN/LOCODE and then by a name or alias that fits exactly one port. Case, spaces and punctuation do not matter, so "GB FXT" and "gbfxt" both find Felixstowe. A partial name never counts.

That is how the tanker NORDIC TRADER, waiting at the anchorage with "FELIXSTOWE" as its destination, shows under Expected before it has moved towards the port at all.

Expected: the tanker at the anchorage, matched to Felixstowe by the name it reports.

docs.title: It does not cry wolf
docs.text:
AIS is noisy. A corrupted message can put a ship on the wrong side of the world, and a weak signal leaves gaps. Places are built to ignore that:

  • A position has to be believable. One the ship could not have reached from its last at 60 knots is left out, unless the next one agrees with it.
  • A crossing needs two positions. A ship enters when two positions in a row, at least ten seconds apart, are inside. One stray position across the line changes nothing.
  • Silence does not end a stay. A ship heard again after an hour, still inside, keeps its original arrival time.
  • A call needs a stop. The fishing boat ORWELL FISHER sailed straight across the anchorage and is listed as nearby, not inside. Only the tanker at anchor counts.

Haven anchorage: the tanker at anchor counts, the fishing boat passing through does not.

docs.title: Places in the other tools
docs.text: Everything above is available to other programs as well. The arrivals and departures are events, the ships inside a place are a list, and each ship has its visits. The next part asks the station about them, over HTTP and in plain words.

  • Quick Start: install AIS-catcher and see your first ships, in a few steps.
  • Places: every place type and every property of a place file, with examples.

docs.title: 1. Multiple Receivers and Stations
docs.text: Part 1 Multiple receivers Part 2 Geofencing Part 3 API and MCP Part 4 Home automation

docs.title: Running multiple receivers at one or more stations
docs.text:
Run more than one receiver from one AIS-catcher. Receivers in one place are one station, receivers elsewhere are stations of their own, each with its range and figures, and the ships they hear together form one picture.

Connecting your station to other tools, part 1 · 6 minutes to read

The example: two stations and the ten ships between them, three of them in reach of both antennas; each station counts what it hears, and the map shows them all.

One antenna sees what its horizon allows. A second one, a few miles up the coast or on the other side of a hill, fills in what the first misses. AIS-catcher runs both from one installation. Each place with receivers is a station, with its own position, range and figures, however many receivers stand there, and the ships they hear together form one picture.

Note

The example in this series is a station at Harwich, where the Stour and the Orwell meet the North Sea, and for this part a second one at Orford, about thirteen nautical miles up the Suffolk coast. The ships are a scripted replay in a test installation. Their names and numbers are made up, the behaviour of AIS-catcher is not.

docs.title: Stations and inputs
docs.text:
Two words do the work. A station is a place where receivers stand. An input is what delivers a receiver's messages: a dongle on this machine, or another receiver sending NMEA over the network. They are two lists, in the dashboard and in the configuration alike. Each input names the station it stands at, and a station can have many: two dongles on one mast are two inputs at one station. From then on every message carries the number of its station.

INPUTS Dongle on the roof rtlsdr · 00000001 Second dongle rtlsdr · 00000002 Pi at Orford, over UDP udpserver · port 10110 station 3 station 3 station 5 STATIONS id 3 Harwich 51.94, 1.28 id 5 Orford 52.09, 1.53 AIS-catcher one tracker every message carries its station all ships filter id 3 per station The main map both stations, every ship A filtered server what station 3 heard API, MQTT, health figures for each station Two lists: the inputs, and the stations they stand at. Both dongles at Harwich are station 3. The one tracker keeps the station with every message, so every view can show all stations or just one.

In the dashboard:

  1. Open Settings, then Stations, and press Add station. Give it a name and a position: fixed, from a GPS, or on a vessel for a receiver that sails.
  2. Open Inputs, pick an input and choose its station under Station.
  3. Press Save changes.

A station has a number, a name and a position. The page names the inputs that stand on it.

An input picks its station from the list.

A second antenna rarely sits on the same machine. The usual set-up is a small receiver at the far site, a Raspberry Pi with a dongle, that forwards what it hears over UDP to the central installation:

On the Pi at Orford

AIS-catcher -d 00000001 -u 192.168.1.10 10110

The central machine takes that stream in as an input of its own, standing at the Orford station. In its configuration file:

config.json, on the central machine

"stations": [
    { "id": 3, "name": "Harwich", "lat": 51.94, "lon": 1.28 },
    { "id": 5, "name": "Orford",  "lat": 52.09, "lon": 1.53 }
],
"receiver": [
    { "input": "rtlsdr", "serial": "00000001", "station": 3 },
    { "input": "rtlsdr", "serial": "00000002", "station": 3 },
    { "input": "udpserver", "udpserver": { "port": 10110 }, "station": 5 }
]

Stations are optional. Out of the box every input stands at the default station, numbered 0: one dongle, or several on the same mast, is one station, and nothing needs setting up. Stations matter once receivers stand in different places.

docs.title: What you see in the browser
docs.text:
The map shows both stations with their range rings, and every ship either of them hears. Distance and bearing are measured from the station that heard the ship, so each antenna's range stands on its own.

Harwich in the south, Orford in the north: ten ships, heard by one station or both.

A ship in reach of both lists both, on the AIS tab of its card.

ORWELL STAR, heard at Harwich and at Orford.

Click a station and its card opens: the ships it hears, its message rate, whether it is receiving, how far it reaches, and an Activity strip of the last 24 hours. While the card is open the map looks through that station alone, and the header says so. Close the card and the full picture is back.

The Harwich card. The map now shows what Harwich hears, and the header names the station.

To stay with one station longer, pick it under Filter in the viewer's settings. The statistics can be read per station too: messages, ranges and plots for one station, or Plots, Compare to set two against each other.

docs.title: One station on a server of its own
docs.text:
Sometimes one station belongs to someone else: a sailing club's antenna on the harbour wall, say, and the club would like a map of its own. That is not a viewer per station but a filter. Add a server under Services and switch on its filter for that station: the server keeps the ships the station hears, and its markers, pages and figures are that station's.

config.json

"services": [
    { "port": 8120, "bind": "0.0.0.0", "filter": "on", "id": 3 }
]

The server filtered on Harwich: six ships, against the ten on the full map.

docs.title: Private by default
docs.text: Where an antenna stands is often someone's house. A station's position stays on the machine unless you switch on Share position on its page. Without it, no map, API, MQTT topic or webhook says where the station is, and the community map keeps it private too. Ranges and bearings are still measured from it, on the machine itself.

docs.title: Stations in the other tools
docs.text:
The station travels with every message, so the tools in the next parts know it too:

  • The API lists the stations under /api/v1/stations with the vessels each heard in the last hour, /api/v1/stations/{id}/statistics gives one station's figures, and /api/v1/vessels?stations=5 gives the ships one station heard.
  • Home Assistant gets an online sensor and a vessel count for each station.
  • Health warns when a station has heard nothing for 15 minutes, so a dead antenna at the far site does not go unnoticed.

Next: geofencing, the areas on the map that turn positions into arrivals and departures.
