  • Locate your station: the set-up guide for a station and its position.

docs.title: Send Ships to Your Chart Plotter
docs.text:
AIS-catcher can pass every message it receives on to OpenCPN, a chart plotter or a navigation app on your network, as NMEA over UDP. The ships then appear on that program's chart.

You need: AIS-catcher receiving ships, and the address of the computer or plotter that should get them. Port 10110 is the usual port for AIS.

On the same computer?

If the chart plotter runs on the same computer as AIS-catcher, use the address 127.0.0.1.

docs.title: On the command line
docs.text:
Add -u with the address and the port to the command you already use:

AIS-catcher -u 192.168.1.20 10110

To give the output a name in the statistics, add description "Chart plotter" after the port.

docs.title: In a configuration file
docs.text:
Add a udp entry:

{
  "config": "aiscatcher",
  "version": 1,
  "udp": [
    { "host": "192.168.1.20", "port": 10110, "description": "Chart plotter" }
  ]
}
Key What it does host, port Where the receiving program listens. description The output's name in the statistics.

Then restart AIS-catcher with the file:

AIS-catcher -C config.json

From the command line to a configuration file

Add -J to print your command line as a configuration file instead of running it: AIS-catcher -u 192.168.1.20 10110 -J.

docs.title: Set up the chart plotter
docs.text: Tell the receiving program to listen for NMEA over UDP on the same port. In OpenCPN: Options → Connections → Add Connection, choose Network, protocol UDP, port 10110, and data protocol NMEA 0183.

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
• The ships appear on the plotter's chart within a minute. Names can take a few minutes longer: ships send them less often than their position.

  • With the web viewer on, open Statistics. Under Data Throughput, the output's Bytes out keeps growing.

No ships on the plotter?

  • Bytes out grows: AIS-catcher is sending. Check the port in the plotter and the firewall on that computer. UDP gets no reply, so AIS-catcher cannot tell whether anything is listening.
  • Dropped grows instead: AIS-catcher cannot send to that address. Check the address, and that both machines are on the same network.

docs.title: More
docs.text:
• Several programs: add a -u for each one, or an entry to the udp list for each one.
  • Every device on the network: use the network's broadcast address and switch broadcast on: -u 192.168.1.255 10110 broadcast on, or "broadcast": true in the udp entry.
  • Programs that connect in: some programs want to connect to AIS-catcher themselves. Use a TCP server output for those.
  • Every UDP setting is in the UDP reference.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text: On the command line, every setting is a switch: a dash and a letter, often followed by values. AIS-catcher does what the switches say and nothing else.

docs.title: Check the install
docs.text:
See which receivers this build supports:

AIS-catcher -L

See which receivers are connected:

AIS-catcher -l

docs.title: A first run
docs.text:
AIS-catcher -v 10

AIS-catcher starts the first receiver it finds, shows each message on the screen, and prints statistics every 10 seconds. With several receivers connected, pick one by its number in the -l list, or by its serial number:

AIS-catcher -d:1 -v 10
AIS-catcher -d 00000001 -v 10

docs.title: How a command line is built
docs.text:
A switch takes its values, then any settings as name and value pairs. This sends messages over UDP and names the output:

AIS-catcher -u 192.168.1.20 10110 description "Chart plotter"
  • Switches can repeat. Two -u switches are two UDP outputs.
  • Settings follow their switch. They apply to the switch before them, until the next switch.
  • Names are not case-sensitive on the command line: RTLAGC on and rtlagc on are the same. Put a value with spaces in quotes.
  • An unknown setting stops AIS-catcher with unknown setting "...", so a typo never goes unnoticed.

Receiver settings go with a -g switch, whose second letter names the device:

AIS-catcher -gr tuner 33.3 rtlagc on
Switch Device Switch Device -gr RTL-SDR -gt RTL-TCP -gm Airspy -gy SpyServer -gh Airspy HF+ -gz ZMQ -gd HydraSDR -ge Serial port -gf HackRF -ga Raw file -gs SDRplay -gw WAV file -gu SoapySDR -go The decoding model

Every switch and setting is in the reference: inputs, decoding and outputs.

docs.title: From the command line to a file
docs.text:
-J writes the command line as a configuration file instead of running it:

AIS-catcher -gr tuner 33.3 -u 192.168.1.20 10110 -J config.json

Without a file name, it prints the configuration on the screen. -C reads a file back, and can be combined with other switches:

AIS-catcher -C config.json -v 10

docs.title: Every switch
docs.text:
AIS-catcher -h prints this list:

use: AIS-catcher [options]

    [-a xxx - set tuner bandwidth in Hz (default: off)]
    [-b benchmark demodulation models for time - for development purposes (default: off)]
    [-c [AB/CD] - [optional: AB] select AIS channels and optionally the NMEA channel designations]
    [-C [filename] - read configuration settings from file]
    [-D [connection string] - write messages to a database: libpq string, sqlite:[file] or csv:[directory]]
    [-e [baudrate] [serial port] - read NMEA from serial port at specified baudrate]
    [-E [config file] [bind address:port] [TLS_CERT file TLS_KEY file] - managed mode: engine run from config file with control server, must be only option (defaults: config.json, control port 8118, viewer on control port + 1, local access without password; use 0.0.0.0:port for LAN access with password)]
    [-f [filename] write NMEA lines to file]
    [-F run model optimized for speed at the cost of accuracy for slow hardware (default: off)]
    [-G [LEVEL level] [SYSTEM on] - control logging (levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL) or enable system logging]
    [-h display this message and terminate (default: false)]
    [-K - print a new API key with its SHA-256 and how to use it, and terminate]
    [-J [file] - write this command line as a configuration file and terminate: to the file, or the screen without one; -C reads it, -E runs it in managed mode]
    [-H [optional: url] - send messages via HTTP, for options see documentation]
    [-i [interface] - read NMEA2000 data from socketCAN interface - Linux only]
    [-I [interface] - push messages as NMEA2000 data to a socketCAN interface - Linux only]
    [-m xx - run specific decoding model (default: 11, engine v2; 2 is engine v1), see README for more details]
    [-M xxx - set additional meta data to generate: T = NMEA timestamp, D = decoder related (signal power, ppm) (default: none)]
    [-n show NMEA messages on screen without detail (-o 1)]
    [-N [optional: port][optional settings] - a web server at port: the map, and api, mcp, system, geojson, kml or metrics switched on; with a message filter it keeps ships of its own; TLS_CERT file TLS_KEY file for HTTPS; KEYS name:scopes:sha256[:limit],... for access by key (scopes data or data+system, limit requests a minute); see README for details]
    [-o set output mode (0 = quiet, 1 = NMEA only, 2 = NMEA+, 3 = NMEA+ in JSON, 4 JSON Sparse, 5 JSON Full (default: 2)]
    [-O MMSI - sets the own mmsi of the receiver]
    [-p xxx - set frequency correction for device in PPM (default: zero)]
    [-P xxx.xx.xx.xx yyy - TCP destination address and port (default: off)]
    [-q suppress NMEA messages to screen (-o 0)]
    [-s xxx - sample rate in Hz (default: based on SDR device)]
    [-S xxx - TCP server for NMEA lines at port xxx]
    [-T xx - auto terminate run with SDR after xxx seconds (default: off)]
    [-u xxx.xx.xx.xx yyy - UDP destination address and port (default: off)]
    [-v [option: xx] - enable verbose mode, optional to provide update frequency of xx seconds (default: false)]
    [-W url [key value]... - events to a webhook (http, https), or the station's state to Home Assistant over MQTT (mqtt, mqtts, ws, wss); keys as in the configuration file, lists comma-separated]
    [-X connect to AIS community feed at www.aiscatcher.org (default: off)]
    [-Q publish data to MQTT server]
    [-Z lat lon - set receiver location (latitude and longitude in decimal degrees)]

    Device selection:

    [-d:x - select device based on index (default: 0)]
    [-d xxxx - select device based on serial number]
    [-e baudrate port - open device at serial port with given baudrate]
    [-l list available devices and terminate (default: off)]
    [-L list supported SDR hardware and terminate (default: off)]
    [-r [optional: yy] filename - read IQ data from file or stdin (.), short for -r -ga FORMAT yy FILE filename
    [-t [[protocol]] [host [port]] - read IQ data from remote RTL-TCP instance]
    [-w filename - read IQ data from WAV file, short for -w -gw FILE filename]
    [-x [server][port] - UDP input of NMEA messages at port on server
    [-y [host [port]] - read IQ data from remote SpyServer]
    [-z [optional [format]] [optional endpoint] - read IQ data from [endpoint] in [format] via ZMQ (default: format is CU8)]

    Device specific settings:

    [-ga RAW file: FILE [filename] FORMAT [CF32/CS16/CU8/CS8] ]
    [-gd HydraSDR: SENSITIVITY [0-21] LINEARITY [0-21] VGA [0-14] LNA [auto/0-14] MIXER [auto/0-14] BIASTEE [on/off] ]
    [-ge Serial Port: PRINT [on/off] FLOWCONTROL [none/hardware/software] INIT_SEQ [string] ]
    [-gf HACKRF: LNA [0-40] VGA [0-62] PREAMP [on/off] ]
    [-gh Airspy HF+: THRESHOLD [low/high] PREAMP [on/off] ]
    [-gm Airspy: SENSITIVITY [0-21] LINEARITY [0-21] VGA [0-14] LNA [auto/0-14] MIXER [auto/0-14] BIASTEE [on/off] ]
    [-gr RTLSDRs: TUNER [auto/0.0-50.0] RTLAGC [on/off] BIASTEE [on/off] ]
    [-gs SDRPLAY: GRDB [0-59] LNASTATE [0-9] AGC [on/off] ]
    [-gt RTLTCP: HOST [address] PORT [port] TUNER [auto/0.0-50.0] RTLAGC [on/off] FREQOFFSET [-150-150] PROTOCOL [none/rtltcp] TIMEOUT [1-60] ]
    [-gu SOAPYSDR: DEVICE [string] GAIN [string] AGC [on/off] STREAM [string] SETTING [string] CH [0+] PROBE [on/off] ANTENNA [string] ]
    [-gw WAV file: FILE [filename] ]
    [-gy SPYSERVER: HOST [address] PORT [port] GAIN [0-50] ]
    [-gz ZMQ: ENDPOINT [endpoint] FORMAT [CF32/CS16/CU8/CS8] ]

    Model specific settings:

    [-go Model: AFC_WIDE [on/off] FP_DS [on/off] PS_EMA [on/off] SOXR [on/off] SRC [on/off] DROOP [on/off] DD_TRAIN [weight] DD_WEIGHT [weight] ]

docs.title: AIS-catcher-control
docs.text:
AIS-catcher-control is a separate package for Raspberry Pi and Debian-based systems that starts and stops the AIS-catcher process and manages the host from the browser. Configuration of the receiver itself is done in AIS-catcher's own dashboard — AIS-catcher-control is the tool around it: service control, one-click updates and reboot.

Note

Earlier versions of AIS-catcher-control included full configuration menus (device, outputs, data flow). This functionality has been superseded by managed mode; AIS-catcher-control now focuses on controlling the process and the host. On other platforms the process is managed with the native tools instead — e.g. Docker containers via Docker itself.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
First install AIS-catcher itself via the install script, then install AIS-catcher-control as a separate service:

sudo bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jvde-github/AIS-catcher-control/main/install_ais_catcher_control.sh)"

docs.title: Accessing the Interface
docs.text:
Open your web browser and navigate to the machine's address on port 8110, for example: http://raspberrypi.local:8110

Default password

Log in with the default password admin — you will be asked to set your own password right after. Systems upgraded from an earlier installation keep their previously set password.

docs.title: Controlling the Service
docs.text:
Navigate to Control to manage the AIS-catcher service:

  • Start/Stop the service.
  • Enable Auto-Start functionality.
  • Monitor the service status through the live log stream (colour-coded by level: error, warning, notice, info, debug).

docs.title: System Management
docs.text:
The System section shows host information (load, memory, disk, AIS-catcher and Control versions) and lets you:

  • check for updates of both AIS-catcher and AIS-catcher-control;
  • start the update / install scripts and watch their progress live;
  • reboot the host or reset a failed service;
  • inspect the optional reboot watchdog status (enabled via the install script).

docs.title: Configuration File
docs.text:
A configuration file holds the same settings as the command line, written as JSON. Load it with -C:

AIS-catcher -C config.json

-C reads the file where it stands on the command line, so other switches can go with it: AIS-catcher -C config.json -v 10. To start from a command line you already use, let -J write the file for you: see Command Line.

docs.title: A complete example
docs.text:
One RTL-SDR, a web viewer on port 8100, a UDP output and the community feed:

{
  "config": "aiscatcher",
  "version": 1,
  "sharing": true,
  "receiver": [
    { "input": "rtlsdr", "rtlsdr": { "tuner": "auto", "rtlagc": true } }
  ],
  "server": [
    { "port": 8100, "station": "My station", "lat": 52.1, "lon": 4.3 }
  ],
  "udp": [
    { "host": "192.168.1.20", "port": 10110, "description": "Chart plotter" }
  ]
}

Every file starts with "config": "aiscatcher" and "version": 1. With nothing else, AIS-catcher picks a receiver as it does on the command line.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
• Keys are lowercase, and case-sensitive.
  • Outputs are lists: udp, tcp, http and the others take one entry per output.
  • "active": false switches a section off and keeps its settings. Leave it out and the section is on.
  • A value can be a number or a string: 10110 and "10110" are the same.

docs.title: The main section
docs.text:
Key What it holds Reference config, version "aiscatcher" and 1; required receiver The receivers, one object each below stations Where the antennas stand below sharing, sharing_key The community feed Community Feed screen, verbose, verbose_time What the screen shows Console Output udp, tcp, tcp_listener UDP, TCP client and TCP server outputs UDP, TCP client, TCP server http, mqtt HTTP and MQTT outputs HTTP, MQTT db Databases Database server Web viewers Web Viewer tracking, services The ship tracker and the servers that read it below webhooks Addresses each event is posted to Webhooks mqtt_state The station's state on an MQTT broker Home Assistant

The generated Configuration Keys list every key with its type, default and values.

docs.title: Receivers (receiver)
docs.text:
Each entry of receiver is one receiver. input picks the kind of device, and a section of the same name holds its settings:

{
  "config": "aiscatcher",
  "version": 1,
  "receiver": [
    { "input": "rtlsdr", "serial": "00000001", "description": "Mast" },
    { "input": "rtlsdr", "serial": "00000002", "description": "Mast, long range",
      "channel": "CD", "engines": [ { "type": "v1_high" } ] }
  ]
}
Key What it does Reference input The kind of device: rtlsdr, airspy, serialport, udpserver and so on Inputs serial Picks one device of that kind by its serial number description The receiver's name in the viewer and the statistics station The number of the station in stations it stands at Stations lat, lon Its position, when it names no station channel AB, the standard pair, or CD, the long-range pair Long Range AIS sample_rate, bandwidth, freqoffset The settings every SDR has Inputs engines The decoders, each { "type": ... } with optional settings Decoding, Engines verbose, meta, own_mmsi Statistics on the screen, extra metadata, the station's own MMSI Console Output rtlsdr, airspy, … The device section matching input Inputs

A device section configures a device but does not select it: input does. A single receiver can also stand in the main section itself, as -J writes it: "rtlsdr": { ... } at the top level.

docs.title: Stations (stations)
docs.text:
A station is where an antenna stands. Every ship's distance and bearing, and the range figures, are measured from the station that heard the ship, so receivers at different places each measure from their own. The viewer's own lat and lon are only used for a receiver that has no position.

Each entry of stations has a number and may have a name, a position and an altitude:

Key Type Description id number Unique; what a receiver names in its station key. 0 is the default station: where every receiver stands that names none name string Shown in the viewer; Station <id> when left out lat, lon number Decimal degrees; both or neither alt number Height of the antenna in metres mmsi number The vessel the station is on: it is wherever that vessel last reported, and gps does not apply gps boolean Whether GPS sentences move the station; off unless set to true. Its lat and lon are then where it stands until the first fix share_loc boolean Whether the station's position may leave this machine, for a server that does not say so itself with its own share_loc. Off unless set: no server, API or map then shows where it is, nor which vessel it rides, nor how far or in which direction a vessel it heard lies from it. The station's own range figures (furthest vessel, maximum distance, radar) still go to its owner: a browser on the station itself, or an API key with system scope. Which vessels a station hears still hints at its general area

A message that names a station itself, as a feed from a hub does in its tag block, counts at that station when stations lists it, else at the input's.

Stations are optional. A receiver that names none stands at the default station, 0: list it to give it a name and a position like any other, or leave it out and it is made when the run starts, named after the one receiver standing on it when that has a description, else after the viewer's station, and placed where a receiver with lat and lon of its own is, else where the viewer section puts it (lat, lon, alt, share_loc, use_gps, own_mmsi). A receiver may also say "station": 0. Once the file has a stations list, every message carries the number of its station as station_id, 0 included. An engine of a receiver may carry a station of its own ("settings": { "station": 2 }, -go station 2 on the command line), so two decoders of one input are told apart: each then has its own figures, and Plots → Compare sets one against the other.

{
    "config": "aiscatcher",
    "version": 1,
    "stations": [
        { "id": 1, "name": "Harbour mast", "lat": 52.10, "lon": 4.27, "alt": 20 }
    ],
    "receiver": [
        { "input": "rtlsdr", "serial": "ab", "station": 1 },
        { "input": "rtlsdr", "serial": "cd", "station": 1, "channel": "CD" },
        { "input": "udpserver", "udpserver": { "port": 10110 }, "description": "Pier" }
    ]
}

Here the two dongles share the antenna on the harbour mast, and the UDP input stands at the default station, named after it. The log lists what each receiver became:

Receiver 1: station 1 "Harbour mast" at 52.099998, 4.270000
Receiver 2: station 1 "Harbour mast" at 52.099998, 4.270000
Receiver 3: station 0 "Pier", no position

A station that moves. A receiver on a boat, or one with a GPS attached, does not stay where the file puts it. A station's position comes from one source at a time: the vessel its mmsi names, else GPS when gps is true, else its lat and lon.

  • A station with an mmsi rides that vessel: each position the vessel reports, heard by any receiver, moves the station there.
  • A station with "gps": true moves with the GPS sentences ($GPRMC, $GPGGA and the like) arriving on the inputs of the receivers that name it. When no receiver names it, GPS on any input moves it.
  • The default station, when the file does not list it, moves with GPS on the inputs standing on it unless the viewer's use_gps is off; listed, it follows its own gps like any other.
  • The position in the file is where a moving station starts, until the first fix. Ships are measured from where the station was when it heard them. The last fix is kept in the tracking backup, so a restart does not send a station back to its configured position.

These apply to the stations of the tracker and the services below, which report each station's position with its source (configured, gps or vessel) and the time of the last fix. The viewer under server keeps its own single position, set by lat, lon, use_gps and own_mmsi as before.

docs.title: Tracking and services (tracking, services)
docs.text:
AIS-catcher keeps one picture of everything its receivers hear, the tracker, and offers it through services: a list of servers, each a port and what it serves: the web viewer, the API, MCP, the system service, GeoJSON, Prometheus. The tracker is built when the file has a server; without one nothing is kept. The viewer of -N and of a server section is such a server too. Both are part of the standard builds; a build made with cmake -DAPI=OFF leaves them out and refuses these keys.

{
    "config": "aiscatcher",
    "version": 1,
    "stations": [ { "id": 1, "name": "Harbour mast", "lat": 52.10, "lon": 4.27 } ],
    "receiver": [ { "input": "rtlsdr", "station": 1 } ],
    "tracking": { "file": "/var/lib/ais-catcher/tracking.bin", "backup": 10 },
    "services": [
        { "port": 8110, "api": true },
        { "port": 8111, "bind": "0.0.0.0", "ui": false, "api": true,
          "view": { "hidden_buckets": ["bm", "bs"], "seen": 30, "track_time": 3600 } },
        { "port": 8112, "tracking": { "allow_type": "1,2,3", "history": 3600 } }
    ]
}

tracking, all optional:

Key Type Default Description file string none Backup of ships, statistics, events and station fixes, read at start and written on exit. A backup an earlier version wrote (the file of server, or of -N) is copied once to <file>.before-upgrade, imported, and from then on written over in this version's format. To go back to the earlier version, rename the copy back to the file's name backup number 10 Minutes between backups to file; 0 writes only on exit history number 1800 Seconds a ship is kept after its last message track_time number 3600 Seconds of track kept per ship; 0 is no limit max_ships number 4096 Size of the ship table cutoff number 2500 Distance in nautical miles beyond which a ship does not count towards range track_memory number 1024 Kilobytes of track kept per ship expire boolean false Forget a ship's details when it leaves lat, lon number none Where a message from no known station is measured from places string none A directory of place files: the tracker then keeps every ship's visits, as the viewer does with its own places

Each entry of services, one server:

Key Type Description port number Required; one server per port active boolean false switches the server off: it keeps its settings, which are still checked, but opens no port and keeps no ships. On unless set bind string Address to listen on; 127.0.0.1 unless set, so a server is reachable from other machines only when you say so. Beyond this machine, a server with api, mcp or system needs keys or public ui boolean The web viewer, on unless set false; with it the viewer's own options (realtime, station, station_link, mbtiles, …), see Web Viewer api boolean The read API under /api/v1: stations, statistics, vessels with their tracks and visits, places with the ships inside and their visits, aircraft, and events. See API. A server limited to some stations serves no aircraft, as aircraft are not kept by station mcp boolean The same for an assistant, at /mcp system boolean Receivers, outputs, health and the log, under /api/v1/system geojson boolean The ships as GeoJSON at /geojson metrics boolean Message counts for Prometheus at /metrics; prome says the same share_loc boolean Whether this server shows where the stations are: their positions, each vessel's distance and bearing, and the range. A server that does not say goes by each station's own share_loc limited boolean The short form for whoever asks: lists of 25 rows at most, vessel rows without the station, one vessel in full without its stations, and 25 data calls an hour from one address. Off unless set tracking object Ships of the server's own, behind a filter on the messages: the terms of an output's filter (allow_type, block_mmsi, stations, unique, …) and zone or groups_in for the receivers that feed it, with history and track_time for what it keeps. The backup and the places are the site's. Without it the server reads the site's tracker. A server whose filter names stations (stations, or id on the command line) shows those stations alone: their markers, pages and figures keys array The keys the server accepts, each { "name", "sha256", "scopes" }: see Keys public boolean Its data is for anyone, without a key; never its system view object Which ships this server shows of what its tracker keeps, and how far back: stations, mmsi_allow, mmsi_deny, hidden_buckets, hidden_classes, hidden_statuses, speed_min, speed_max, distance_min, distance_max, seen (minutes since heard), validated, repeated, track_time (seconds of track served, at most what the tracker keeps), and place_geometry (false serves places with their marker position only, keeping their outlines on this machine; on unless set). What it leaves out no route of the server sends: the map, the API, MCP and GeoJSON. A view never makes a tracker; only a message filter does (filter on with its terms, or zone, groups_in). Leave it out to show all

A viewer under server, and -N on the command line, is read as an entry of services: the same server, with the same keys. One without a message filter shows the site's ships, and its file, backup and history are the site's tracking; one with filter on, or with zone or groups_in, keeps ships of its own behind that filter, as the viewer always did, while the backup stays the site's. On the command line the switches follow the port: AIS-catcher -N 8100 api on mcp on.

The filter uses the terms of the web viewer's own filter (Settings → Filter on the map), under the same names, so a filter you set up in the viewer can be copied here as it stands. It selects from everything the tracker keeps: the server shows nothing outside it, in any list, count or event.

Term Type Description stations array Only ships one of these stations heard in the last hour; 0 is a ship no listed station heard hidden_buckets array Groups left out: am, as (class A moving, stationary), bm, bs (class B), aton, base, sarte, air hidden_classes array Ship classes left out, by number: 2 cargo, 3 class B, 4 passenger, 5 special, 6 tanker, 7 high-speed, 8 fishing, 0 everything else hidden_statuses array Navigational statuses left out, 0 to 15; 15 is also a status not reported speed_min, speed_max number Knots; a ship without a speed falls outside either seen number Heard within this many minutes; 0 is any age distance_min, distance_max number Nautical miles from the station that heard the ship validated string any, yes, no or pending repeated string any, only (passed on by a repeater) or never mmsi_allow, mmsi_deny array Only these MMSIs; never these

A request to /api/v1/vessels takes filters of its own, named after the fields of a vessel (?class=cargo,tanker&min_speed_kn=1). They narrow what the server shows and never widen it.

docs.title: How Manual Mode Works
docs.text: In manual mode, AIS-catcher does exactly what you tell it when you start it: on the command line, or in a configuration file. There is no dashboard and nothing changes while it runs. To change a setting, stop AIS-catcher, change the command or the file, and start it again.

docs.title: A first run
docs.text:
AIS-catcher -v 10

That is a complete AIS receiver. AIS-catcher starts the first receiver it finds, shows each message on the screen, and prints statistics every 10 seconds.

docs.title: Command line or configuration file
docs.text:
Both hold the same settings, so pick the one that suits the job:

  • Command line: quick to type and to try. Good for a first run and for experiments.
  • Configuration file: one JSON file, loaded with -C. Good for a station that runs for months, for several receivers, and for keeping your settings in one place.

To move from one to the other, let AIS-catcher write the file:

AIS-catcher -gr tuner auto -u 192.168.1.20 10110 -J config.json
AIS-catcher -C config.json

-J writes the command line as a configuration file instead of running it, and -C runs the file.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Command Line: how a command line is built, and every switch.
  • Configuration File: how the file is laid out.
  • Running as a Service: start AIS-catcher at boot on Linux and the Raspberry Pi.
  • The reference: every setting of the inputs, the decoding and the outputs.

Set up from the dashboard in your browser instead? That is managed mode: see the dashboard.

docs.title: Running as a Service
docs.text:
On Linux and the Raspberry Pi, the install script without -M sets AIS-catcher up as a systemd service in manual mode. The service runs as the user aiscatcher and reads two files:

  • /etc/AIS-catcher/config.json, a configuration file.
  • /etc/AIS-catcher/config.cmd, command-line switches, one or more per line. Lines starting with # are comments.

AIS-catcher reads config.json first, then the switches in config.cmd. Outputs in both files add up; a setting in both takes the value from config.cmd. Put your settings in whichever file you prefer:

sudo nano /etc/AIS-catcher/config.cmd

docs.title: Start, stop and check
docs.text:
Restart the service after changing either file:

sudo systemctl restart ais-catcher.service
Command What it does sudo systemctl start ais-catcher.service Start it sudo systemctl stop ais-catcher.service Stop it sudo systemctl enable ais-catcher.service Start it at boot sudo systemctl disable ais-catcher.service Do not start it at boot systemctl status ais-catcher.service Show whether it runs journalctl -u ais-catcher.service -f Follow its log
